title: Advanced Rheumatology Fellowships
level: Adult internal-medicine rheumatology fellowship (Johns Hopkins directory label/umbrella; not a separate advanced subspecialty)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: For study: prior graduate-level foundation in adult internal medicine, clinical epidemiology, pharmacology and basic immunology; ability to read guidelines critically.

For the actual Johns Hopkins fellowship, the programme page states MD/DO/MD-PhD, completed accredited internship and internal-medicine residency by enrolment, ERAS application and NRMP specialty match requirements.
For ABIM certification: meet ABIM’s separate Internal Medicine certification, accredited fellowship, competence, licensure and examination requirements; this study plan provides none of them.

No learner should perform aspiration, polarized-light microscopy, injection, immunosuppressive prescribing or patient triage based on this material without the appropriate licensed, supervised setting.
objectives: Use pattern- and organ-threat-based reasoning across the ABIM rheumatology blueprint.
Interpret public guidelines with population, certainty, conditionality and patient-specific limitations explicit.
Distinguish a clinical fellowship’s supervised rotations/procedures from independent video study.
Critically evaluate de-identified, licensed image/case resources without copying or rehosting protected images.
Communicate uncertainty, red flags and escalation needs in fictional educational cases.

units.title: Immune mechanisms, inflammation and the rheumatologic consultation
objectives: Relate innate/adaptive immune pathways, complement and autoantibodies to clinical syndromes.
Frame a consult around urgency, pattern, host factors and a test that changes management.
Explain why a public lecture cannot substitute supervised examination or patient care.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional fever-and-polyarthritis stem to build a differential; do not use a real chart.
units.assessment: 10-item mechanism/diagnostic-reasoning quiz; cite the uncertainty of each test.

units.title: Musculoskeletal examination, synovial fluid and imaging reasoning
objectives: Distinguish inflammatory from mechanical and periarticular patterns from history and examination.
Interpret why synovial fluid microscopy, microbiology and imaging answer different questions.
State the supervised-procedural boundary for aspiration, polarized microscopy and injection.
topics: plain film, US, MRI and DXA indications
units.casePractice: MedPix search: inflammatory arthritis/rheumatoid arthritis; inspect record-level de-identification and license before use.
units.assessment: Interpretation worksheet that separates a diagnostic inference from a management decision.

units.title: Crystal arthritis, septic arthritis and related arthritides
objectives: Compare gout, CPPD and basic calcium phosphate disease with infectious arthritis.
Use synovial-fluid findings without treating a crystal finding as exclusion of infection.
Summarize guideline-level gout principles and limits of independent-study use.
units.casePractice: Fictional hot-knee case: formulate urgent work-up and escalation, not a home treatment plan.
units.assessment: Short-answer comparison of crystals, culture and clinical risk; original MCQ Q2–Q3.

units.title: Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory polyarthritis
objectives: Recognize patterns that support RA while considering mimics and infection.
Connect disease activity, comorbidity, pulmonary disease and shared decision-making to longitudinal planning.
Describe the 2021 ACR recommendation context for initial DMARD-naive moderate-to-high disease activity without writing prescriptions.
units.casePractice: Analyze the public RA-ILD grand-rounds recording with a guideline cross-check; do not treat the transcript as an individualized recommendation.
units.assessment: One-page evidence-to-case map and original MCQ Q4.

units.title: Spondyloarthritis, psoriatic disease and regional pain
objectives: Differentiate axial/peripheral spondyloarthritis from mechanical, infectious and crystal disease.
Identify extra-articular features and referral/co-management questions.
Avoid overcalling MRI or HLA findings outside clinical context.
units.casePractice: Open-i licensed-filter search for psoriatic arthritis imaging; retain source link and license, not a copied image.
units.assessment: Pattern-recognition comparison table plus original MCQ Q5.

units.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome
objectives: Organize SLE by organ threat, activity/damage, pregnancy and thrombotic differential.
Explain evidence-based treatment goals and glucocorticoid minimization at a conceptual level.
Recognize when aPL positivity, APS and catastrophic presentations require specialist/emergent evaluation.
boardDomains: Other Rheumatic and Connective Tissue Disorders (16.5%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional nephritic-sediment SLE case to identify organ-threatening features and multidisciplinary needs.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal of the EULAR recommendations plus original MCQ Q6.

units.title: Systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, Raynaud phenomenon and connective-tissue disease
objectives: Differentiate primary from secondary Raynaud patterns and organize systemic-sclerosis organ screening questions.
Compare sicca symptoms with Sjögren syndrome and alternative causes.
Recognize pulmonary, renal and vascular red flags requiring specialist co-management.
boardDomains: Other Rheumatic and Connective Tissue Disorders (16.5%)
units.casePractice: Use MedPix/Open-i only through source links; do not export an image or make a diagnosis from a single image.
units.assessment: Structured differential and safety checklist.

units.title: Inflammatory myopathies, autoinflammation and systemic manifestations
objectives: Differentiate inflammatory, metabolic, medication-associated and critical-illness myopathies.
Recognize dysphagia, respiratory and cardiac involvement as escalation triggers.
Relate IL-1 biology and innate inflammation to autoinflammatory reasoning without extrapolating investigational claims.
boardDomains: Other Rheumatic and Connective Tissue Disorders (16.5%)
units.casePractice: Fictional proximal-weakness case: distinguish data needed for diagnosis from a treatment order.
units.assessment: Original MCQ Q7 and an annotated differential.

units.title: Vasculitides and urgent mimics
objectives: Classify large-, medium-, small- and variable-vessel vasculitis and identify urgent organ-threatening presentations.
Distinguish AAV from infection, embolic disease, malignancy, drug-related disease and other mimics.
Interpret the 2021 ACR/VF GPA/MPA recommendations as conditional guidance, not a protocol for unsupervised use.
units.casePractice: Fictional pulmonary-renal syndrome: state stabilization, cultures/serology/urinalysis/imaging/biopsy questions and emergency specialist escalation.
units.assessment: Original MCQ Q8 and a red-flag triage memo.

units.title: Metabolic bone disease, osteoarthritis and noninflammatory mimics
objectives: Contrast osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget disease and CKD-related bone disease at a high level.
Differentiate OA and regional pain from inflammatory arthritis while acknowledging coexistence.
Interpret DXA and fracture-risk outputs only in clinical context.
units.casePractice: Open-i license-filter exercise for OA/osteoporosis images; do not infer fracture risk from an image alone.
units.assessment: Image-context worksheet and original MCQ Q9.

units.title: Therapeutics, infection prevention, reproductive health and longitudinal care
objectives: Compare medication classes by mechanism, monitoring question, infection risk and patient values at a conceptual level.
Build a pre-immunosuppression safety checklist that includes infection, vaccination, malignancy, organ function and reproductive goals.
Use shared decision-making and health-equity considerations in case discussion.
units.casePractice: Fictional pre-biologic visit: identify questions that require a clinician/pharmacist and what cannot be decided by this course.
units.assessment: Safety checklist scored with a transparent rubric.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, professionalism and fellowship-to-practice boundaries
objectives: Appraise a guideline’s population, strength, certainty and applicability.
Describe what clinical rotations, continuity clinic, supervision and procedure documentation provide that video study cannot.
State exact ABIM eligibility boundaries and avoid claiming certification from this course.
units.casePractice: Write a de-identified fictional consult handoff and disclose uncertainty, escalation and supervision requirements.
units.assessment: Capstone evidence-to-case brief plus original MCQ Q10.

assignment.title: De-identified fictional consult-to-evidence portfolio
components: Create four fictional one-page cases: hot monoarthritis, inflammatory polyarthritis/possible RA, organ-system SLE or systemic sclerosis, and vasculitic red flags.
For each, state problem representation, dangerous alternatives, discriminating data, uncertainty, consultation/escalation needs and two source-linked claims.
Review one MedPix or Open-i resource by link only; record license/attribution, de-identification statement, and why it cannot be rehosted by default.
Write a 500-word guideline appraisal comparing strength/certainty/applicability; do not write patient-specific orders.
assignment.submissionBoundary: No real patient records, identifiers, screenshots, protected images, copied board items, clinical orders or procedure claims.

formative: 12 unit checks (retrieval questions, image-context notes, evidence-to-case maps).
10 original practice questions in this record; these are not ABIM items and do not predict passing.
Peer/self rubric emphasizes uncertainty, safety and source use rather than diagnosis certainty.
assessment.passingOrCredentialNotice: No grade confers credit, fellowship completion, board eligibility, procedure competence, licensure, certification, CME/MOC credit, affiliation or guaranteed passing.

studyHours.note: This is a transparent independent-study plan. The 36-hour video floor is met only by observed unique public recording durations; clinical rotations, conferences, original planned clips and reading time are not counted as external ready video hours.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medicine
mapping.name: Advanced Rheumatology Fellowships (directory title); linked Rheumatology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Directory: Johns Hopkins Hospital, “Non-Standard” accrediting-body field, duration 1–3 years. Linked Division page: two-year ACGME-accredited Rheumatology Fellowship; research-duration sources conflict: overview says an additional T32 year, while clinical/research pages describe two additional years after year one. Year 1: inpatient blocks at Johns Hopkins Hospital/Bayview; ambulatory general rheumatology, lupus, arthritis, myositis, scleroderma, vasculitis, Sjögren’s and ultrasound clinics; allied-field electives. Year 2 clinical-excellence pathway: disease-center clinics plus longitudinal clinic, with optional USSONAR/education training. Investigative pathway: additional two years, coursework/research, continuity clinic plus a research-aligned center clinic. These are official programme descriptions, not online lectures or guarantees of current availability.

topicGaps: The 38-hour public grand-rounds ledger meets the numeric floor, but 31 title-only recordings do not disclose a disease topic; they are not used as evidence for specific board-domain coverage.

No verified public, fellow-level recording was found for supervised joint aspiration/injection, validated polarized-light microscopy or hands-on musculoskeletal ultrasound; these cannot be replaced by a clip.
No public recording ledger verifies the full local Johns Hopkins core curriculum, proprietary conference slides, case volume, patient encounters or procedure competency.
Guidelines and drug indications change; re-check primary source versions and local policy before clinical use.

medical.trackType: Adult internal-medicine rheumatology fellowship (Johns Hopkins directory label/umbrella; not a separate advanced subspecialty)
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) – Rheumatology Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: ABIM has a Rheumatology Certification Examination. “Advanced Rheumatology Fellowships” is not a separately named ABIM certification, subspecialty examination or additional board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABIM states that rheumatology certification requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification, completion of accredited fellowship training, documented competence, a valid unrestricted/un-challenged medical license and passing the examination. Training must be ACGME, Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, or Collège des médecins du Québec accredited. ABIM lists 24 months total training and 12 clinical months, plus specified aspiration/microscopy and injection procedures. An online course, public videos, research time alone, observation or a clinical rotation cannot be substituted or double-counted. The separate ABIM/ABAI combined rheumatology–allergy/immunology pathway requires prospectively approved three-year combined training; no claim is made that Johns Hopkins offers it.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Advanced Rheumatology Fellowships (directory title); linked Rheumatology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Directory: Johns Hopkins Hospital, “Non-Standard” accrediting-body field, duration 1–3 years. Linked Division page: two-year ACGME-accredited Rheumatology Fellowship; research-duration sources conflict: overview says an additional T32 year, while clinical/research pages describe two additional years after year one. Year 1: inpatient blocks at Johns Hopkins Hospital/Bayview; ambulatory general rheumatology, lupus, arthritis, myositis, scleroderma, vasculitis, Sjögren’s and ultrasound clinics; allied-field electives. Year 2 clinical-excellence pathway: disease-center clinics plus longitudinal clinic, with optional USSONAR/education training. Investigative pathway: additional two years, coursework/research, continuity clinic plus a research-aligned center clinic. These are official programme descriptions, not online lectures or guarantees of current availability.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is an actual Johns Hopkins directory record, but “Advanced Rheumatology Fellowships” is a local plural directory label, not a distinct ABMS specialty or separate board. The directory labels its accrediting body “Non-Standard”; the linked Division page identifies the underlying adult Rheumatology Fellowship as a two-year ACGME-accredited programme and describes an additional research pathway. This entry transparently studies adult internal-medicine rheumatology fellowship-level knowledge and the local clinical/research variants; it does not create an “advanced rheumatology” certification.
sourceCaveats: The dynamic ACR topical hub pages returned minimal text in the research extractor; primary guideline full texts were used for clinical claims instead.
The original user outline was unrelated nuclear-medicine material and was not imported. Its unsupported case-volume/equipment/board claims have no role in this rheumatology entry.
The Johns Hopkins directory’s “Non-Standard” field applies to the directory entry; the linked division page separately states that the two-year underlying Rheumatology Fellowship is ACGME accredited.
Rheum.TV is explicitly a Johns Hopkins patient-education platform and was not counted as fellow-level video curriculum.

Public YouTube duration metadata was observed from the channel listing. Some individual video pages were later rate-limited in the research environment, so availability must be rechecked before assignment; no content was downloaded, rehosted or counted twice.

The imported individual UW transcript was reliable for the RA-ILD title/topic but the myopathy transcript was poor quality. The ledger therefore uses only title-level topic identity unless a topic was explicit in public metadata.
No clinical expert reviewed this independent-study artefact; date-check recommendations, labels and local policy at the point of use.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the January 2026 ABIM Rheumatology Certification Blueprint, which single medical content category has the largest target percentage on a typical exam?

options.text: Rheumatoid arthritis
Lupus erythematosus
Vasculitides
Basic and clinical sciences

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint assigns rheumatoid arthritis 13%, larger than lupus (9%), vasculitides (8.5%), and basic/clinical sciences (7%). Blueprint percentages are an assessment specification, not a clinical-priority ranking.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 63-year-old has an acutely hot knee and synovial fluid with needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals. Fever and marked systemic inflammation are present. Which reasoning step is best?

options.text: Crystals exclude infection, so culture is unnecessary.
Treat the crystal finding as a complete explanation and defer further evaluation.
Maintain concern for infection and incorporate microbiologic evaluation and urgent clinical assessment as indicated.
Diagnose rheumatoid arthritis from the crystal morphology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A crystal finding does not, by itself, rule out concurrent infection. The ABIM blueprint separately includes synovial-fluid analysis and infections/related arthritides; real-time assessment and testing require a treating team.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the 2020 ACR gout guideline for patients in whom urate-lowering therapy is indicated?

options.text: Use pegloticase as first-line therapy for all patients.
Use a low starting dose and titrate urate-lowering therapy to a serial serum-urate target below 6 mg/dL, with prophylaxis when initiating therapy.
Stop clinically indicated low-dose aspirin solely to lower urate.
Avoid allopurinol in every patient with CKD stage 3 or worse.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline strongly recommends allopurinol as preferred first-line ULT including in CKD stage 3 or worse, low-dose initiation with titration, a serum-urate target below 6 mg/dL, and prophylaxis for 3–6 months when starting ULT. This is educational guideline recall, not a patient-specific prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the 2021 ACR RA guideline, which initial strategy is strongly recommended over hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, biologic/targeted synthetic monotherapy, and several combinations for DMARD-naive moderate-to-high disease activity?

options.text: Methotrexate monotherapy
Chronic glucocorticoid monotherapy
A biologic DMARD before any conventional DMARD in all cases
No disease-modifying treatment until erosions appear

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2021 guideline strongly recommends methotrexate monotherapy in that defined population. Application requires contraindication, reproductive, infection, organ-function and preference assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has chronic inflammatory back pain, alternating buttock pain, uveitis history and psoriasis. Which answer best describes the next reasoning task?

options.text: Diagnose axial spondyloarthritis solely from one symptom.
Integrate axial and peripheral pattern, extra-articular features, differential diagnoses and appropriately selected tests.
Classify all back pain as nonrheumatic.
Treat an HLA result as diagnostic without clinical context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABIM blueprint includes axial, peripheral, psoriatic, reactive and IBD-associated spondyloarthritis with skeletal and extra-articular manifestations. Classification tools and tests must be interpreted within clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement matches the 2023 EULAR SLE recommendations summarized in the cited source?

options.text: Maintenance glucocorticoids should routinely be continued indefinitely at high dose.

Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients at a target of 5 mg/kg real body weight/day while individual flare and retinal-toxicity risk are considered; maintenance glucocorticoids should be minimized and, when possible, withdrawn.
Organ-threatening disease never needs immunosuppressive therapy.
All patients with SLE receive exactly the same regimen.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This is the cited recommendation summary. It is not a dosing instruction for an individual; selection and monitoring require clinician oversight.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has progressive proximal weakness, dysphagia and elevated muscle enzymes. What is the most appropriate course-level conclusion?

options.text: A single enzyme value establishes an inflammatory myopathy subtype.
The presentation needs a structured differential and urgent clinical assessment of bulbar/respiratory involvement; educational material cannot replace diagnostic evaluation.
Dysphagia is irrelevant to myopathy assessment.
All proximal weakness is rheumatoid arthritis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint includes idiopathic inflammatory, metabolic, medication-associated and critical-illness myopathies. Dysphagia and respiratory involvement are safety-relevant and require real clinical assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: Other rheumatic and connective tissue disorders

practiceQuestions.stem: Which option best matches the 2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation recommendation for active severe GPA or MPA?

options.text: Rituximab is conditionally recommended over cyclophosphamide for remission induction.
Plasma exchange should routinely be added for every presentation.
Glucocorticoid-free observation is recommended for all severe disease.
ANCA titer alone establishes every management decision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline conditionally recommends rituximab over cyclophosphamide for active severe GPA/MPA and conditionally recommends against routine plasma exchange in the cited scenarios. Conditional recommendations require individualized specialist judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which procedural statement is required by ABIM for rheumatology certification training, but cannot be fulfilled by this independent course?

options.text: Demonstrated diagnostic aspiration with light and polarized microscopy of synovial fluid and therapeutic injection competence.
Watching 36 hours of public videos.
Completing an unsupervised online anatomy quiz.
Joining a public video channel.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM specifies those procedural requirements. The course offers no procedure authorization, supervision, observed competence or training credit.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the Johns Hopkins pathway connected from the directory entry?

options.text: The directory label creates a separate “Advanced Rheumatology” ABIM board.

Year one includes inpatient blocks and ambulatory clinics; the linked program describes a two-year ACGME-accredited rheumatology fellowship, with an research pathway available; its published duration is inconsistent across the official Hopkins pages.
The research pathway eliminates any need for supervised clinical training for ABIM certification.
The independent course is affiliated with Johns Hopkins.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The linked Johns Hopkins pages describe those clinical components and the two-year ACGME fellowship with added research training. The directory calls its own accrediting field “Non-Standard”; the local directory label is not a new board.

title: Allergy and Clinical Immunology Fellowship Program

prerequisites.level: Post-residency physician-fellow cognitive study; not a substitute for medical school, residency, supervised fellowship or independent practice.
requiredKnowledge: Medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, microbiology and immunology.
Ability to read guidelines and appraise evidence.
Prior supervised adult/pediatric acute-care experience assumed for conceptual cases only.
technical: Use captions/transcripts where provided; do not redistribute video/patient images.
prerequisites.safety: Never perform skin testing, spirometry, food/drug challenge, desensitization, allergen/venom immunotherapy, immunoglobulin prescribing, biologic administration, emergency medication administration or genetic interpretation from this course. These need authorised supervision and systems.

objectives: Map published ABAI domains to a transparent, non-proprietary plan.
Explain core immune/type-2 mechanisms and limits.
Use phenotype, timing, exposure and pretest probability for differentials.
Distinguish sensitization testing from clinical allergy.
Summarize evidence principles across airway, skin, food, anaphylaxis, venom, drug and immune deficiency.
Recognize red flags requiring emergency/supervised evaluation.
Describe—not perform—ACGME clinical/procedural competencies.
Appraise guideline date, population, uncertainty and conflicts.
Apply systems, stewardship, quality and equity thinking to fictional cases.
State why this course cannot confer fellowship equivalence or certification.

units.title: Immune architecture, tolerance, and type-2 inflammation
objectives: Differentiate innate, adaptive, barrier and neuroimmune contributions to allergic inflammation.
Connect antigen presentation, IgE, mast cells, eosinophils and cytokines to clinical phenotypes.
Separate mechanistic plausibility from treatment recommendation.
units.casePractice: Fictional seasonal-wheeze/rhinitis mechanism map; no diagnosis from a test alone.
units.assessment: Concept map plus early-versus-late-response explanation.

units.title: Allergen exposure, testing, and probability-aware interpretation
objectives: Elicit exposure, timing and symptom history before interpreting tests.
Explain why sensitization alone does not establish clinical allergy.
Specify when diagnostic procedures require supervised teams.
units.casePractice: Fictional seasonal-rhinitis history; distinguish sensitization from relevance.
units.assessment: History checklist and interpretation rationale.

units.title: Upper and lower airway disease: rhinitis, asthma, sinus disease, and AERD
objectives: Build differentials for rhinitis and cough including non-allergic causes.
Interpret the conceptual role and limits of PFT evidence.
Describe AERD without encouraging self-challenge.
units.casePractice: Fictional asthma/polyps/NSAID reaction: red flags, alternatives and referral questions.
units.assessment: PFT-report concept exercise and safety-boundary statement.

units.title: Skin disease and delayed hypersensitivity
objectives: Differentiate atopic dermatitis, urticaria, angioedema, irritant and allergic contact dermatitis by timing/morphology.
Explain why patch testing needs clinical correlation.
Use guideline awareness without treating a person.
units.casePractice: Link-only DermNet comparison: view under host terms, never copy images.
units.assessment: Morphology/timing differential table.

units.title: Food allergy, prevention, challenge reasoning, and eosinophilic GI disease
objectives: Differentiate food allergy, intolerance, sensitization and clinical reactivity.
Explain the supervised oral-food-challenge boundary.
Date-label NIAID prevention guidance and recognize local care may differ.
units.casePractice: Fictional parent-reported reaction history: targeted questions/referral, not home challenge.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal and safety script.

units.title: Anaphylaxis, venom allergy, and mast-cell disorders
objectives: Apply current anaphylaxis principles including timely epinephrine concepts.
Differentiate local sting reactions, systemic reactions and anaphylaxis conceptually.
State specialist scope for recurrent or idiopathic episodes.
units.casePractice: Paper emergency-recognition scenario; no emergency treatment or procedure.
units.assessment: Time-critical recognition quiz and tryptase-timing exercise.

units.title: Drug, vaccine, and biologic hypersensitivity
objectives: Classify immediate and delayed adverse-drug reactions by phenotype/timing.
Use probability-based concepts to explain inaccurate labels.
State supervision/emergency requirements for challenge and desensitization.
units.casePractice: Fictional penicillin label classification only; no challenge/delabeling.
units.assessment: Risk-stratification memo cited to 2022 parameter.

units.title: Primary and secondary immunodeficiency
objectives: Organize antibody, combined/T-cell, phagocyte, complement and secondary mechanisms.
Recognize patterns requiring specialist assessment.
Explain that Ig orders and genetics interpretation are supervised activities.
units.casePractice: Fictional recurrent-infection phenotype: mechanism differential and escalation plan.
units.assessment: Laboratory-pattern worksheet and referral rationale.

units.title: Immune dysregulation, eosinophilia, and immune therapeutics
objectives: Differentiate deficiency from immune dysregulation, autoimmunity and inflammatory phenotypes.
Explain mechanisms/monitoring concepts without individual regimens.
Recognize eosinophilic presentations needing multidisciplinary care.
units.casePractice: Fictional eosinophilia vignette: mechanism questions and referrals.
units.assessment: Mechanism-to-manifestation evidence table.

units.title: Clinical reasoning, procedures, safety, and interprofessional care
objectives: Describe but do not perform ACGME procedural competencies.
Explain why logs, direct observation and emergency systems cannot be replaced by video.
Frame stewardship, handoffs and cost-conscious care as systems work.
units.casePractice: Simulated handoff for fictional uncertain antibiotic reaction.
units.assessment: QI mini-protocol naming authorised supervisors.

units.title: Research methods, evidence appraisal, and equity
objectives: Formulate focused questions and distinguish guideline, observational, mechanistic and opinion evidence.
Identify date, population, conflicts, applicability and uncertainty.
Incorporate values, access and disparities in hypothetical discussion.
units.casePractice: Critique a guideline statement and explain uncertainty in plain language.
units.assessment: PICO, evidence table and 500-word appraisal.

units.title: Integrated case conference and blueprint synthesis
objectives: Synthesize allergy, airway, skin, food/drug and immune-deficiency evidence without premature closure.
Map a portfolio to the public ABAI blueprint without predicting an exam.
State supervised-training/eligibility gaps precisely.
boardDomains: All public ABAI domains; curricular mapping only
units.casePractice: Two fictional composite cases with evidence map and escalation boundary.
units.assessment: 50 original formative items and portfolio self-rubric.

assignment.title: Evidence-anchored integrated case portfolio (fictional composites only)
deliverables: Mechanism map (Unit 1).
Three probability-aware differentials: airway/skin, food/anaphylaxis, drug/immunodeficiency.
One dated practice-parameter appraisal and current-source check.
One interprofessional safety/QI reflection naming authorised supervisors.
Two fictional capstones with alternatives, source map, uncertainty and emergency/supervision boundary.
assignment.rules: No real patient record, identifiable story, image, diagnostic order, treatment plan, procedure attempt, protected board item or paywalled/protected download. Each vignette must be labelled fictional.

formative: Interpretation worksheets for published concepts, not actual patient reports.
Self-rubric informed by public milestones, not an official assessment.
summative: Capstone portfolio scored for reasoning, source quality, alternatives, safety boundary, equity and uncertainty.
assessment.notValidation: No assessment is an ABAI examination, validates clinical competence, awards CME/credit, predicts a passing score or replaces a Clinical Competency Committee.

unitMap.text: Immune architecture, tolerance, and type-2 inflammation
Allergen exposure, testing, and probability-aware interpretation
Upper and lower airway disease: rhinitis, asthma, sinus disease, and AERD
Skin disease and delayed hypersensitivity
Food allergy, prevention, challenge reasoning, and eosinophilic GI disease
Anaphylaxis, venom allergy, and mast-cell disorders
Drug, vaccine, and biologic hypersensitivity
Primary and secondary immunodeficiency
Immune dysregulation, eosinophilia, and immune therapeutics
Clinical reasoning, procedures, safety, and interprofessional care
Research methods, evidence appraisal, and equity
Integrated case conference and blueprint synthesis

topicGaps: 18.300833 hours remain below the 36-hour free, unique, duration-verified recording target; no new candidate had a reproducible exact runtime at this check.

Additional relevant public lecture pages were identified, but runtime evidence could not be established; one candidate is now private, and an official listing points to an unrelated video. These are excluded rather than estimated.

Source-backed scripts address mechanisms, probability-aware interpretation, airway differential, drug reaction phenotyping, and immune-deficiency pattern reasoning; other blueprint areas still need current, topic-specific freely available teaching, especially contact dermatitis, FPIES/EoE, venom, pediatric disease, immune dysregulation, tests/procedures, research methods and equity.

No public recording set replaces complete Johns Hopkins protected didactics/conferences or ACGME-supervised clinical continuity, direct observation, case/procedure logs, emergency response, faculty evaluation, research mentorship or credentialing.
Guidelines, approvals, indications and safety communications require recurrent date checks; human clinician review was not performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: ABAI is the relevant ABMS member board. Its public blueprint (updated Nov 2021) is a coverage guide, not secure exam content. ABIM/ABP are qualifying boards, not issuers of an ABIM/ABP A/I certificate.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent study creates NO ACGME credit, competency documentation, procedure log, programme attestation, ABIM/ABP certification, unrestricted licence, ABAI eligibility, “board eligibility,” certification, credential or right to sit an exam. medical.programmeSourceScope: Actual separate clinical physician fellowship, not a generic category. Transparent study scope: adult/pediatric A/I cognitive study mapped to published ABAI/ACGME domains. Johns Hopkins Track 1 is stated to lead to ABAI board eligibility; Track 2 is research intensive and expressly not for A/I board certification. NIAID rotation descriptions are separately labelled comparison only, never claimed as Hopkins rotations.
sourceCaveats: All programme/guideline sources were opened directly; no conclusion rests only on snippets.

topicGaps: 18.300833 hours remain below the 36-hour free, unique, duration-verified recording target; no new candidate had a reproducible exact runtime at this check.

Additional relevant public lecture pages were identified, but runtime evidence could not be established; one candidate is now private, and an official listing points to an unrelated video. These are excluded rather than estimated.

Source-backed scripts address mechanisms, probability-aware interpretation, airway differential, drug reaction phenotyping, and immune-deficiency pattern reasoning; other blueprint areas still need current, topic-specific freely available teaching, especially contact dermatitis, FPIES/EoE, venom, pediatric disease, immune dysregulation, tests/procedures, research methods and equity.

No public recording set replaces complete Johns Hopkins protected didactics/conferences or ACGME-supervised clinical continuity, direct observation, case/procedure logs, emergency response, faculty evaluation, research mentorship or credentialing.
Guidelines, approvals, indications and safety communications require recurrent date checks; human clinician review was not performed.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has recurrent severe episodes consistent with anaphylaxis. Which timing plan best aligns with the 2023 parameter for assessing tryptase?

options.text: Only a baseline years later is useful.
Draw an acute sample as early as possible, ideally within 2 hours of onset, and a later baseline comparator.
Draw only after epinephrine fails.
A normal value proves no anaphylaxis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 parameter suggests acute tryptase as early as possible, ideally within two hours, plus a baseline comparator. It supports assessment but does not replace clinical judgement or emergency care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult’s only childhood “penicillin allergy” symptom was isolated nausea. Which statement best reflects the 2022 drug-allergy parameter?

options.text: Skin testing is mandatory before any beta-lactam.
The history is inconsistent with allergy; routine testing is not recommended, though a one-step amoxicillin challenge may be considered for reassurance in an appropriate supervised setting.
The label proves IgE-mediated allergy.
A home dose escalation is appropriate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: For histories inconsistent with allergy, the parameter recommends against routine testing; any reassurance challenge is a supervised clinical decision, never a self-study task.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which allocation is explicitly described in the ACGME Allergy and Immunology requirements?

options.text: 50% direct patient care/case conferences/record review; 25% scholarship/research; 25% other educational activities.
100% direct patient care.
50% research and 50% lectures only.
A fixed 36 video hours.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME describes the 50–25–25 distribution; it does not prescribe 36 video lecture hours.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which age distribution is specified for direct patient-care activity?

options.text: Only adult care.
Only pediatric care.
At least 20% birth–18 years and at least 20% older than 18 years.
Exactly half every clinic pediatric.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 ACGME requirements set at least 20% pediatric and 20% adult direct-patient-care activity. This course supplies neither.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which major public ABAI blueprint section has the largest stated weight?

options.text: Emerging priorities, 1%.
Allergy and Hypersensitivity Principles and Disorders, 54%.
Pharmacology, 2%.
Immune system/research, 9%.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public blueprint lists 54%; it is a guide, not a secure examination prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient asks whether a video can replace specialist evaluation or venom immunotherapy after a systemic sting reaction. Best response?

options.text: Yes; self-administer extract after watching.
Yes; online score determines venom/dose.
No; video may support learning but testing, risk assessment and immunotherapy require supervised clinical care and emergency systems.
No care is needed after any sting reaction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Stinging insect allergy is an ACGME clinical-experience domain. A video cannot provide testing, treatment, supervision or emergency support.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is an ACGME FAQ minimum procedure number?

options.text: 30 PFT interpretations.
300 unsupervised food challenges.
100 independent biologic infusions.
No procedures need documentation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The FAQ lists 30 PFT interpretations, 10 written immunotherapy prescriptions, 10 desensitization/incremental challenges, 30 immediate skin tests, 5 Ig prescriptions and 5 food challenges—supervised programme requirements only.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional food-exposure episode includes rapidly progressive respiratory symptoms. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Wait for every diagnostic criterion before epinephrine.
Response to epinephrine proves diagnosis.
Criteria need not be met before epinephrine; emergency management should not wait for a retrospective label.
Antihistamine is always an equivalent first-line substitute.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 parameter says criteria are not required before epinephrine and response is not a diagnostic surrogate. A suspected emergency needs local emergency action.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which Johns Hopkins track distinction is correctly stated?

options.text: Both tracks confer ABAI eligibility.
Track 1 is described as leading to ABAI eligibility; Track 2 is research intensive and explicitly not intended for A/I board certification.
Track 2 is an additional ABIM certificate.
Neither includes research.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Johns Hopkins public didactics describes Track 1 and explicitly excludes board-certification intent from Track 2; actual eligibility remains ABAI-governed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which additional bundle is required by ABAI for initial certification beyond passing the exam?

options.text: Any online review course.
ABIM and/or ABP certification at exam date, qualifying fellowship, documentation, references and unrestricted licence as specified by ABAI.
36 online-video hours.
A simulated conference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABAI specifies these requirements. This course cannot attest any of them.

title: Allergy/Immunology Fellowship
prerequisites: Appropriate advanced health-sciences background (e.g., medical-school level physiology, pathology, pharmacology and evidence appraisal).
Working knowledge of adult and pediatric history-taking, physical examination, asthma basics and infection differential diagnosis.
For licensed clinical action, only one’s own credentialing, supervision, institutional policy and current guidance apply; course participation grants none.
Learners without clinical training may study concepts but must not perform or interpret procedures for patient care.
objectives: Map current ABAI published blueprint domains to mechanisms, disease phenotypes, tests and evidence appraisal.
Reason from clinical history and pretest probability to testing limitations rather than equating sensitization with disease.
Recognize safety boundaries in suspected anaphylaxis, food/drug reactions, immunodeficiency and severe asthma.
Distinguish independent study from ACGME training, clinical supervision, licensure and ABAI certification.
Locate and date-check primary guidance before making a management claim.

units.title: Immune-system architecture, innate defense, and clinical translation
objectives: Relate barriers, innate cells and lymphoid organs to host defense.
Explain how innate and adaptive responses shape inflammatory phenotypes.
Separate normal immune variation from clues that warrant an immune-deficiency evaluation.
topics: barriers; complement; phagocytes; cytokines; organs; host defense
units.casePractice: Create a mechanism-first differential for a fictional child with recurrent sinopulmonary infections; do not diagnose a real person.
units.assessment: 10-item mechanisms quiz plus a one-page host-defense concept map.

units.title: Antigen recognition, antibodies, MHC, and laboratory reasoning
objectives: Explain antigen presentation, B/T-cell development and antibody diversity.
Interpret the purpose and limitations of immunoglobulin, functional-antibody, complement, lymphocyte-subset and flow-cytometry tests in a clinical question.
Avoid treating an isolated laboratory abnormality as a diagnosis.
topics: immunoglobulins; MHC; antigen presentation; B cells; T cells; flow cytometry; test limitations
boardDomains: Clinical and laboratory tests in ABAI item classification
units.casePractice: For a fictional recurrent-infection vignette, justify a staged test plan and state what each result cannot establish.
units.assessment: Short-answer interpretation exercise, scored for indication, limitation and next question.

units.title: Allergy history, sensitization testing, and supervised challenge concepts
objectives: Elicit a chronology-driven allergy history and distinguish sensitization from clinical allergy.
Compare skin, serum and challenge-based approaches conceptually, including false-positive/false-negative risk.
Recognize that challenges and skin testing are clinical procedures requiring appropriate setting, supervision and local protocol.
topics: pretest probability; skin testing; serum IgE; false positives; oral food/drug challenges; documentation
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional histories that have the same positive sensitization test but different pretest probabilities.
units.assessment: Structured test-selection rationale; explicitly list a limitation and a safety escalation point.

units.title: Allergen exposure reduction and immunotherapy principles
objectives: Explain allergen identification, avoidance and environmental-control reasoning.
Describe indications, selection and safety concepts for allergen immunotherapy without treating this course as procedure authorization.
Distinguish education about an intervention from independent prescribing or administration.
topics: aerobiology; extracts; allergen avoidance; immunotherapy principles; monitoring
units.casePractice: Draft an evidence-question worksheet for a fictional seasonal-rhinitis history, including alternative explanations for symptoms.
units.assessment: Concept map linking exposure, phenotype, test meaning and safe referral.

units.title: Rhinitis, sinus disease, ocular allergy, and environmental aeroallergens
objectives: Build a differential for allergic and non-allergic rhinitis and chronic sinonasal symptoms.
Relate pollen/spore seasonality to a history without assuming causation.
Identify when asthma, sinus, ocular or occupational symptoms require broader evaluation.
topics: allergic/non-allergic rhinitis; chronic rhinosinusitis; ocular disease; pollen; molds; indoor allergens
units.casePractice: Use a fictional symptom calendar to formulate competing seasonal and perennial hypotheses.
units.assessment: Timed differential-and-testing plan.

units.title: Asthma phenotypes, pulmonary testing, severe disease, and biologics
objectives: Integrate symptom pattern, spirometry concept, exposures and comorbidity into asthma assessment.
Describe why difficult-to-treat and severe asthma need confirmation of diagnosis, adherence/technique/exposures and specialist evaluation.
Compare therapeutic classes at a conceptual level and use current guidance rather than stale videos as the final authority.
topics: asthma; spirometry; severe asthma; AERD; biologics; comorbid disease
units.casePractice: Interpret a fictional pre-/post-bronchodilator spirometry narrative and list what additional data are needed before phenotype labeling.
units.assessment: Guideline-navigation exercise; cite current GINA section and explain why a video alone is insufficient.

units.title: Atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, urticaria, and angioedema
objectives: Differentiate eczematous, contact, urticarial and angioedema presentations from common mimics.
Explain the role and boundaries of patch testing and immediate hypersensitivity testing.
Recognize when recurrent angioedema or systemic symptoms require urgent/specialist evaluation.
topics: atopic dermatitis; patch testing; contact hypersensitivity; chronic urticaria; angioedema; dermatologic differential
boardDomains: A.5 Anaphylaxis and mast-cell activation disorders (10%)
units.casePractice: Classify fictional lesions by timing, morphology and associated symptoms; identify data that would change the differential.
units.assessment: Image-free morphology/timing table and rationale.

units.title: Food allergy, non-IgE food disorders, eosinophilic GI disease, and challenge reasoning
objectives: Distinguish food allergy from intolerance and recognize the limits of broad panel testing.
Describe the diagnostic role—not an at-home substitute—of an oral food challenge.
Compare immediate food reactions, FPIES and eosinophilic GI disease conceptually.
topics: food allergy; FPIES; oral food challenge; EoE; elimination diets; labeling; prevention
units.casePractice: Use a fictional meal-associated reaction history to identify what is known, what is uncertain and when supervised evaluation is required.
units.assessment: Food-label literacy exercise plus diagnostic-boundary quiz.

units.title: Anaphylaxis, insect venom, mast-cell disorders, and emergency systems
objectives: Apply published diagnostic criteria as aids while recognizing that epinephrine should not wait for all criteria to be met in a suspected event.
Differentiate anaphylaxis, isolated urticaria/angioedema and alternative causes using timing and organ-system involvement.
Explain the rationale for post-event evaluation and emergency action planning without giving patient-specific emergency orders.
topics: anaphylaxis criteria; tryptase concepts; insect venom; mastocytosis; mast-cell activation; action plans
boardDomains: A.5 Anaphylaxis and mast-cell activation disorders (10%)
units.casePractice: Map organ-system features in a fictional acute reaction and identify the emergency escalation versus later diagnostic questions.
units.assessment: Safety-first scenario response, graded on recognition of emergency escalation and uncertainty.

units.title: Eosinophilic, autoinflammatory, autoimmune, and immune-inflammatory disorders
objectives: Organize a differential for eosinophilia by clinical context and mechanism.
Recognize the intersection of allergy/immunology with autoimmunity, immune dysregulation and GI disease.
Read evidence with attention to phenotype, differential diagnosis and referral boundaries.
topics: hypereosinophilia; eosinophilic GI disease; autoimmunity; inflammation; IBD
units.casePractice: Create a fictional eosinophilia work-up matrix that lists allergic, infectious, medication, malignant and inflammatory alternatives.
units.assessment: Evidence-table critique; no claim of a definitive diagnosis from a single biomarker.

units.title: Primary and secondary immunodeficiency, infection patterns, and immune therapeutics
objectives: Recognize recurring infection patterns, immune dysregulation and red flags for primary/secondary immunodeficiency.
Select a mechanism-linked initial evaluation conceptually and interpret findings in clinical context.
Describe the role of immunoglobulin replacement, genetics and advanced therapies as specialist-directed care, not self-study permissions.
topics: CVID; SCID; inborn errors of immunity; complement; phagocytes; genetics; immunoglobulin; secondary immunodeficiency
units.casePractice: Work through the licensed Immunopaedia primary-immunodeficiency cases by link only; distinguish findings from diagnosis and note local-resource constraints.
units.assessment: Mechanism-to-test matching exercise and referral/escalation reflection.

units.title: Drug and vaccine hypersensitivity, stewardship, evidence appraisal, and lifelong learning
objectives: Phenotype a reported drug reaction by timing, symptoms and severity; distinguish challenge from desensitization conceptually.
Explain why a history-based risk assessment is central and why unverified labels can cause harm.
Use vaccine contraindication/precaution tables accurately and identify when specialist input is appropriate.
Appraise an article or guideline using question, comparator, outcome, applicability and harms.
topics: drug allergy; delabeling; drug challenge; desensitization; vaccine reactions; contraindications; research design; equity
units.casePractice: For a fictional remote benign drug eruption, write history questions, red flags and why an unsupervised home challenge is outside this course.
units.assessment: Guideline-concordance memo with a source citation and stated uncertainty.

assignment.title: Source-anchored diagnostic-reasoning portfolio
deliverables: One fictional recurrent-infection work-up map: phenotype, mechanism hypotheses, selected tests, test limitations and referral/escalation points.
One fictional acute-reaction map separating emergency escalation from later evaluation; no patient-specific dose or treatment order.
One two-page appraisal of a current guideline or primary source, including date, population, recommendation certainty/limitations and relevance.
One blueprint-to-study map allocating topics by ABAI published domains, explicitly noting that it does not establish exam readiness.
assignment.privacyAndSafety: Use only fictional vignettes or linked lawful, de-identified educational cases. Do not upload patient records, identifiers, screenshots, scans, proprietary questions or protected course content.

formative: Peer/instructor discussion limited to de-identified or fictional content
assessment.summativePlan: Portfolio rubric: mechanism and differential (30%), evidence/source accuracy and currency (25%), test/procedure limits and safety boundaries (25%), clarity/equity/reflection (20%). Passing an internal rubric does not predict board performance or verify competence.
assessment.acgmeBoundary: ACGME Milestones are designed for evaluation in ACGME-accredited programs and are not used here for credentialing, graduation or independent-practice determinations.

mapping.name: Allergy/Immunology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a three-year fellowship. Year 1: ambulatory, inpatient and consult services; three ambulatory half-days weekly; weekly adult allergy half-day at Brigham and Women’s Hospital; Boston-wide orientation; weekly Immunology School; and two weekly patient-focused conferences. Years 2–3: mentored laboratory or clinical research with clinical responsibilities minimized. This is a public description, not a reproduction of a private schedule, a claim of ACGME status, or an available clinical rotation.

boardNames: American Board of Allergy and Immunology (ABAI) Certification Examination
ACGME Allergy and Immunology program requirements (training standard; not a certifying board)
medical.boardStatus: ABAI is an ABMS member board. ABAI’s public Certification Examination is a separate, secure, annual computer-based examination (225 items; 7 hours; approximate 25% basic science/75% clinical science). The course is neither endorsed by ABAI nor a board-review course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course creates no eligibility. ABAI publicly requires, among other items, ABIM and/or ABP specialty certification by the examination date; at least 24 consecutive months of full-time qualifying Allergy/Immunology fellowship training; program documentation; recommendations; and valid, current unrestricted U.S./territory/Canada licensure. ABAI Requirements says candidates are “Board Eligible” for five years after qualifying fellowship, but ABAI About Certification says ABAI does not recognize that term and says certification must be achieved within seven years; ask ABAI—not this course—to determine individual eligibility. The course cannot replace MD/DO education, residency, fellowship, supervision, procedure experience, credentialing, licensure, or the secure examination.

officialProgrammes.name: Allergy/Immunology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a three-year fellowship. Year 1: ambulatory, inpatient and consult services; three ambulatory half-days weekly; weekly adult allergy half-day at Brigham and Women’s Hospital; Boston-wide orientation; weekly Immunology School; and two weekly patient-focused conferences. Years 2–3: mentored laboratory or clinical research with clinical responsibilities minimized. This is a public description, not a reproduction of a private schedule, a claim of ACGME status, or an available clinical rotation.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Scope is limited to the single declared Boston Children’s Hospital offering. Its public page describes a three-year Allergy/Immunology Fellowship and its own rotations/didactics/research. This record does not claim a Harvard-wide or national catalogue, infer unlisted institutional variants, or treat the fellowship duration as proof of accreditation.
sourceCaveats: The ABAI blueprint page is marked Updated November 2021; it remains the public source located on the ABAI site. Recheck before any high-stakes use.
ABAI’s Requirements and About Certification pages use potentially inconsistent “Board Eligible” wording/time frames. The course reports both rather than reconciling them; ABAI decides eligibility.
Public video duration/access was observed from YouTube playlist metadata on 2026-10-07. Videos may later change, be removed, gain a restriction or have content superseded by current guidance.
Many source recordings are lectures, not guidelines; current primary guidance in the reading list controls when they conflict.

The programme page describes Boston Children’s activities but does not, in the text reviewed, itself state a current ACGME accreditation decision. Do not infer accreditation from programme length or this course.
A licensed case link is not permission to rehost every image or reuse content outside its stated license. No patient image, scan, record or proprietary case is included in this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult reports eating peanut-containing foods without symptoms but has a positive serum peanut-specific IgE found on a broad panel. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The result alone establishes clinical food allergy.
The result may indicate sensitization; history and appropriately selected evaluation determine clinical relevance.
A broad positive panel proves multiple food allergies.
Food allergy is excluded because prior ingestion was tolerated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A test result must be interpreted with the clinical history; positive sensitization alone is not synonymous with clinical allergy. The course does not direct an unsupervised challenge.
practiceQuestions.domain: A.4 Food and drug allergy / clinical tests

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional acute reaction after a likely allergen exposure, the learner is uncertain whether every published anaphylaxis criterion is met. Which statement best reflects the 2023 practice parameter?

options.text: Epinephrine must wait until all criteria are documented.
Meeting diagnostic criteria is not required before use of epinephrine in a suspected event.
Response to epinephrine proves the diagnosis.
Skin findings are required for anaphylaxis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The parameter suggests that meeting diagnostic criteria is not required before epinephrine and that response should not be used as a diagnostic surrogate. This is educational, not individualized emergency direction; seek emergency services for suspected anaphylaxis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a remote, benign cutaneous reaction label to a beta-lactam but no features of anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous adverse reaction. What is the best learning conclusion?

options.text: All such patients need the same skin-test sequence.
History-based risk stratification matters; guideline-supported direct challenge can be considered in selected low-probability settings by appropriately trained clinicians.
The label should remain permanently without review.
A home re-exposure is the reference standard.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The drug-allergy parameter emphasizes phenotype and risk stratification; drug challenge is a clinical procedure with contraindications and appropriate setting requirements, not a self-study exercise.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional young adult has recurrent sinopulmonary infections, low immunoglobulins, and autoimmune cytopenia. Which approach best fits an immunodeficiency evaluation framework?

options.text: Name CVID from one symptom alone.
Use mechanism-linked immune studies and clinical context, considering infection pattern, antibody function and alternative/secondary causes.
Assume genetic testing identifies all cases.
Exclude immune dysfunction because autoimmunity is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABAI’s public overview includes immunoglobulins, functional antibody measurement, complement and lymphocyte analyses as examples of clinically selected tests. CVID can involve recurrent infections and autoimmunity, but formal diagnosis needs specialist evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement is correctly categorized in CDC’s vaccine contraindication/precaution tables?

options.text: A severe allergic reaction after a prior dose or to a vaccine component is commonly listed as a contraindication for the relevant vaccine.
Every history of any allergy is a contraindication to every vaccine.
A family history of allergy alone proves vaccine anaphylaxis risk.
A contraindication table eliminates the need to identify the specific vaccine and component.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC tables list severe allergic reaction after a prior dose or to a component as a contraindication for many specific vaccines. Details vary by vaccine; consult the current table and specialist resources.

practiceQuestions.stem: The ABAI public content overview uses allergic rhinitis to illustrate an immunotherapy principle. Which sequence is most consistent with that overview?

options.text: Begin immunotherapy before taking an allergy-focused history.
Understand allergen avoidance and medical treatment before considering the more intensive immunotherapy approach.
Use immunotherapy as a substitute for diagnostic reasoning.
Assume all rhinitis is allergic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABAI’s overview explicitly frames appreciation of allergen avoidance and medical treatment before initiation of immunotherapy. Individual candidacy and administration require clinical supervision.
practiceQuestions.domain: B.6 Allergens/extracts; A.1 head and neck

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has episodic wheeze and cough. Which statement best describes spirometry’s role in the course?

options.text: Spirometry is irrelevant when symptoms are intermittent.
It is a lung-function test that can help evaluate asthma in an appropriate clinical context, including before/after medicine testing as described by CDC.
A normal single test proves symptoms are not respiratory.
It independently chooses a biologic medication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes spirometry as measuring exhaled air after a deep breath, before and after asthma medicine. Interpretation and treatment are contextual clinical tasks.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which U.S. labeling statement is correct as of the FDA page checked for this course?

options.text: Sesame is not a major food allergen in the United States.
Sesame became the ninth U.S. major food allergen effective January 1, 2023.
All foods sold at any restaurant must carry a FALCPA-style contains statement.
FDA has established a universal safe threshold for every allergen.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA states that the FASTER Act made sesame the ninth major allergen effective January 1, 2023. The same page notes important scope limits and that FDA has not established a threshold level for any allergens.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional infant has early, severe recurrent infections and abnormal lymphocyte screening results. Which course response is safest?

options.text: Delay referral until several years of observation.
Treat the screen as a confirmed molecular diagnosis.
Recognize possible severe immune dysfunction, escalate promptly within an appropriate clinical system, and pursue specialist-directed confirmatory evaluation.
Use a public video to select transplant conditioning.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SCID and combined immunodeficiencies are in the ABAI blueprint. A screen or pattern warrants timely, supervised specialist evaluation; this course neither diagnoses nor directs transplantation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the difference between the course and ABAI certification?

options.text: Finishing the course makes a learner ABAI-certified.
The course can replace an ACGME fellowship because it has videos.
The published ABAI blueprint can orient study, but certification requires independent board-specified training, credentials, documentation, licensure and a secure examination.
The course can reveal protected examination items.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABAI publishes a blueprint but separately requires ABIM/ABP certification, qualifying training, documents, recommendations, licensure and examination. This independent course cannot confer any of these.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional adult with nonvalvular AF and estimated annual thromboembolic risk at least 2%, which statement matches the 2023 guidance?

options.text: Treat only if AF is persistent.
Base stroke prevention on thromboembolic risk regardless of AF pattern; DOACs are generally preferred except with mitral stenosis or mechanical valve.
Use aspirin/clopidogrel instead of anticoagulation for all.
Use a bleeding score alone to deny therapy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidance bases therapy on risk regardless of AF pattern, does not use bleeding scores alone, and gives stated DOAC exceptions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has confusion, tachypnea, hypotension, and a possible urinary infection. What is the educational priority?

options.text: Wait for culture confirmation.
Recognize a life-threatening emergency and arrange immediate clinician evaluation/treatment.
Use leftover antibiotics.
Treat only if fever occurs.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC calls sepsis a life-threatening medical emergency and directs immediate evaluation/treatment; no regimen is supplied.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is CDC’s correct workflow before adult immunization recommendation?

options.text: Age only.
Age table, condition/risk indications, notes, then contraindications/precautions.
Copy a past note.
Use nonclinical web advice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC specifies this sequence.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best reflects ADA patient-centered diabetes scope?

options.text: One identical goal for all.
Assess goals/hypoglycemia with comorbidities, CVD/CKD, access, and preferences.
Only one lab value.
Ignore adverse effects.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ADA covers these linked domains; individual care needs clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which KDIGO 2024 statement is correct?

options.text: Stage by one creatinine only.
Framework includes classification/risk, complications, stewardship and patient-centered care.
One exclusive pathway fits all.
CKD is unrelated to CV risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO describes these domains and says it is not an exclusive standard of care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional inpatient has acute inattention/fluctuating confusion. Safest first framing?

options.text: Assume primary psychiatric illness.
Safety assessment, collateral, medication review, reversible-cause evaluation under supervision.
Wait to discharge.
Normal aging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Delirium is a cross-cutting safety syndrome requiring medical evaluation and supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly separates residency curriculum and ABIM blueprint?

options.text: They are identical.

Watching videos establishes eligibility.
Blueprint is accreditation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Programme, assessment and eligibility sources have different functions.
