title: Clinical Informatics Fellowship
level: Clinical physician subspecialty fellowship; independent board-aligned self-study curriculum-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Prior graduate-level health/clinical sciences, or equivalent informatics and health-system experience; this independent curriculum does not confer admission prerequisites.
Basic probability/statistics and comfort reading tables, workflow diagrams, and structured data.
Ability to distinguish educational self-study from supervised clinical practice and accredited GME.
No real patient data, patient images, protected board questions, live-system testing, or unsupervised patient-care use.
objectives: Explain the physician subspecialty scope and differentiate it from research informatics, general IT, and academic certificates.
Map clinical workflow and sociotechnical system factors before proposing technology.
Design and evaluate CDS and EHR changes using published board domains and safety sources.
Interpret architecture, interoperability, terminology, and data-governance concepts.
Critically assess analytics and AI intended use, data limitations, risks, and monitoring.
Communicate implementation, evaluation, privacy, safety, and leadership tradeoffs.
Build a fictional, source-cited informatics project plan without claiming clinical competence.

units.title: The clinical informatician, informatics science, and health-system context
objectives: Define clinical informatics as a physician subspecialty focused on analyzing, designing, implementing, and evaluating information systems to improve care.
Distinguish clinical informatics from biomedical research informatics, nursing/consumer informatics, data science, general health IT, and an academic certificate.
Represent a clinical information problem in terms of people, process, information, technology, setting, and outcome.
boardDomains: I. Fundamental Knowledge and Skills (20%); V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%)
units.casePractice: Map an entirely fictional outpatient result-follow-up issue across patient, clinician, workflow, information, system, governance, and measurement perspectives; identify what is known and missing.
units.assessment: One-page concept map and 5-item self-check. Rubric: correct scope 30%, explicit stakeholders 25%, evidence/uncertainty 25%, ethical boundary 20%. No operational diagnosis or competence claim.

units.title: Clinical workflows, sociotechnical analysis, and problem framing
objectives: Trace a clinical work process from trigger to downstream action and feedback.
Use stakeholder interviews, observation plans, swim lanes, and task analysis without collecting patient-identifiable information.
Separate a symptom from its causes and define a testable informatics problem statement.
boardDomains: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional referral handoff and map roles, information gaps, queues, delays, and possible failure modes; no real records or interface screenshots.
units.assessment: Submit current-state/future-state swim lanes plus assumptions log. Rubric: process fidelity 30%, users and context 25%, failure-mode clarity 25%, accessibility and uncertainty 20%.

units.title: Quality improvement, measurement, and evidence of effect
objectives: Distinguish structure, process, outcome, and balancing measures.
Create a measure with a clear operational definition, denominator, time window, and data provenance.
Explain why pre/post change alone does not establish causal impact.
boardDomains: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); IV. Data Governance and Data Analytics (15%)
units.casePractice: Use the three linked MIT videos as foundation only. In a fictional result-notification workflow, define process, outcome, and balancing metrics; state ascertainment and missing-data risks.
units.assessment: Measurement plan with numerator, denominator, inclusion rules, frequency, stratification, data source, and balancing measure. Rubric: definitional precision 35%, validity 25%, interpretation 25%, limitations 15%.

units.title: Clinical decision support and safe knowledge management
objectives: Describe the five rights of CDS and map a knowledge artifact into an actual workflow.
Classify CDS intervention formats and assess specificity, timing, actionability, and override burden.
Plan governance, versioning, monitoring, and retirement for a clinical rule.
boardDomains: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%)
units.casePractice: Review the linked AHRQ PSNet alert-fatigue primer and its “Finding Fault With the Default Alert” WebM&M link; produce a link-only annotated discussion. Do not copy case text or any clinical images.
units.assessment: Create a fictional CDS specification and test plan. Rubric: five-rights mapping 25%, workflow fit 25%, safety/harm balancing 25%, governance and monitoring 25%.

units.title: EHR architecture, enterprise systems, and resilience
objectives: Explain a high-level EHR architecture spanning clinical applications, interfaces, APIs, identity, databases, and analytics.
Differentiate transactional clinical systems from downstream reporting/research stores and state risks of latency or semantic drift.
Draft a downtime and recovery tabletop that includes safe data reconciliation and communication.
boardDomains: III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%); I. Fundamental Knowledge and Skills (20%)
units.casePractice: Use ONC 2025 SAFER Contingency Planning and System Management guides as assessment references; scenario and all data are fictional.
units.assessment: Architecture diagram plus tabletop checklist. Rubric: components/flows 30%, boundaries and failure modes 30%, recovery/reconciliation 25%, clarity 15%.

units.title: Interoperability, terminology, and information modeling
objectives: Explain FHIR resources, references, profiles, and implementation guides while distinguishing the base standard from local adoption.
Compare data-exchange concepts across FHIR, HL7 v2, CDA, DICOM, and clinical terminology at a conceptual level.
Identify semantic, identity, provenance, and patient-matching problems that block safe reuse.
boardDomains: I. Fundamental Knowledge and Skills (20%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%); IV. Data Governance and Data Analytics (15%)
units.casePractice: Use public FHIR specification examples only. Map a fictional observation to resource-level concepts; no live service, patient-level data, or claim of implementation conformance.
units.assessment: Annotate a toy schema / JSON example and a data-quality checklist. Rubric: semantic correctness 35%, provenance 25%, interoperability limits 25%, version/profile labeling 15%.

units.title: Data governance, privacy, cybersecurity, and ethical data use
objectives: Apply data stewardship, access control, auditability, and data lifecycle concepts to an informatics project.
Summarize HIPAA Security Rule safeguards without confusing an educational summary with legal advice or compliance attestation.
Recognize privacy, confidentiality, bias, security, and secondary-use questions requiring local governance.
boardDomains: I. Fundamental Knowledge and Skills (20%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%); IV. Data Governance and Data Analytics (15%)
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional de-identified dataset access request. Document purpose, minimum necessary questions, governance, access, security, retention, and uncertainties; do not use actual patient data.
units.assessment: Draft a data access decision memo and risk register. Rubric: legal boundary 25%, governance 25%, security 25%, ethical/data minimization reasoning 25%.

units.title: Analytics, statistics, prediction, and clinical AI
objectives: Choose descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive analytics appropriately and state what each cannot establish.
Describe sampling, missingness, leakage, calibration, discrimination, and distribution shift at a conceptual level.
Frame an AI evaluation with intended use, subgroup analysis, human factors, post-deployment monitoring, and accountability.
boardDomains: IV. Data Governance and Data Analytics (15%); II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%)
units.casePractice: Evaluate a fictional risk-score proposal using no patient data or numeric clinical thresholds. State intended users, workflow, validation population, harms, and monitoring triggers.
units.assessment: Model-card critique and implementation pause/continue recommendation. Rubric: intended-use clarity 20%, evaluation design 30%, equity/safety 30%, monitoring/governance 20%.

units.title: Human factors, usability, and patient-facing informatics
objectives: Plan formative usability testing around representative tasks and diverse users.
Distinguish usability findings from evidence of clinical outcome benefit.
Evaluate patient portals, telehealth, mobile health, and remote-monitoring workflows for access and safety.
boardDomains: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%); V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional portal task-flow storyboard with personas labelled as invented. Do not upload screenshots, patient information, or proprietary interface materials.
units.assessment: Five-task usability protocol, risk log, and prioritized design findings. Rubric: task realism 25%, inclusive design 25%, observation plan 25%, limitations 25%.

units.title: Clinical safety, risk management, and regulatory evaluation
objectives: Use a hazard-analysis approach to identify technology, workflow, and organizational contributing factors.
Distinguish a clinical decision support function from a software function that may be a medical device; follow current FDA guidance rather than categorical claims.
Use ONC SAFER resources to plan local EHR risk review without claiming certification or regulatory compliance.
boardDomains: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%); I. Fundamental Knowledge and Skills (20%)
units.casePractice: Use linked, public AHRQ WebM&M case material by reference only. Discuss system factors, detection, recovery, and learning; never reproduce case images or patient records.
units.assessment: A fictional hazard log with controls and residual risks. Rubric: hazard traceability 30%, human/technical factors 25%, regulatory qualification 20%, monitoring and accountability 25%.

units.title: Leadership, governance, implementation, and organizational change
objectives: Build a stakeholder map and governance path for a hypothetical clinical system change.
Select implementation, training, adoption, and sustainment measures appropriate to the change.
Communicate tradeoffs and uncertainty to clinical, technical, operational, and patient stakeholders.
boardDomains: V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%); II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%); III. Enterprise Information Systems (15%)
units.casePractice: Use only public course/program sources and a fictional project charter. Institutional rotations and committee participation are described, not reproduced as a substitute experience.
units.assessment: Two-page project charter and stakeholder communication brief. Rubric: strategic fit 25%, stakeholder/governance 25%, delivery/change plan 25%, evaluation and risk 25%.

units.title: Capstone: evaluate an informatics intervention and communicate its limits
objectives: Integrate workflow, architecture, data, safety, evaluation, and governance into a bounded project proposal.
Pre-register a pragmatic measure plan and explicit assumptions; distinguish association from causality.
Present a balanced recommendation that includes no-go criteria and post-deployment monitoring.
boardDomains: All five ABPM content areas; emphasis II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes (30%) and V. Leadership and Professionalism (20%)
units.casePractice: Capstone must use a wholly fictional workflow or a public educational case linked in place; no patient-level data, screenshots, protected board items, clinical decisions, or claims of competence.
units.assessment: Portfolio and 10-minute recorded presentation. Rubric: blueprint/evidence map 20%, sociotechnical design 20%, evaluation 25%, safety/privacy 20%, communication/limitations 15%.

assignment.title: Fictional clinical informatics intervention portfolio
deliverables: Blueprint-to-unit and source map with publication/access dates.
Fictional current-state workflow map, stakeholder analysis, system-context diagram and risk register.
A CDS/system design brief with user, task, information, channel, safety controls and governance.
A measurement/evaluation plan defining numerator, denominator, provenance, balancing measures and limitations.
A short capstone communication brief and presentation; use only fictional diagrams or linked public case studies.
assignment.limits: Use fictional scenarios and non-identifiable toy data only. Link authentic public educational cases without copying patient records/images/narratives. No live EHR access or configuration, patient-specific advice, validated competence assessment, or institutional credit.

methods: Original board-domain mapped practice questions with explanatory rationale (30%)
Source-date, access, licensing, and limitations audit (10%)
assessment.passingOrCredentialing: No passing score, CME, ACGME credit, board eligibility, certification, validated board-readiness estimate, clinical evaluation, procedure competence, or patient-care authorization. Questions are original educational items, not official board questions.
assessment.feedback: Self-check against cited public sources and assignment rubric. Any real clinical, legal, security, product-classification, or system-design decision requires appropriate qualified supervisors and local governance.

Clinical workflows, sociotechnical analysis, and problem framing
Quality improvement, measurement, and evidence of effect
Clinical decision support and safe knowledge management
EHR architecture, enterprise systems, and resilience
Interoperability, terminology, and information modeling
Data governance, privacy, cybersecurity, and ethical data use
Analytics, statistics, prediction, and clinical AI
Human factors, usability, and patient-facing informatics
Clinical safety, risk management, and regulatory evaluation
Leadership, governance, implementation, and organizational change
Capstone: evaluate an informatics intervention and communicate its limits

topicGaps: No public board-directed Clinical Informatics fellowship lecture catalogue with observed duration has been verified; the new recordings are broad health-informatics survey talks, not a substitute for ACGME clinical training or a complete ABPM/ABPath review course.

No observed lecture adequately covers the whole ABPM blueprint at board depth. Remaining thin/no-recording areas include detailed privacy/security and legal/ethical governance, full terminology and messaging standards beyond introductory FHIR, research versus transactional analytics, data-quality/stewardship and statistical validation, enterprise architecture/interoperability conformance, organizational budgeting/finance and leadership, implementation/maintenance, and rigorous clinical AI validation and monitoring.

The MIT and Paton recordings broaden systems, EHR/CPOE/CDS, workflow, usability, consumer informatics, AI, FHIR, and improvement exposure; they do not establish depth, currency, board alignment, physician competence, or equivalent coverage of all five blueprint domains.

No accessible complete on-demand recording set was found for Harvard Clinical Informatics Lecture Series; registration-based meetings remain excluded. Public AMIA course announcements were not counted because individual unrestricted lecture access and durations were not established.

21.2897 verified hours remain to the 36-hour target. Published course pages support further learning but not 21.29 hours of qualifying recordings; do not pad or relabel reading time, constructed episodes, or estimated media as verified hours.

medical.boardStatus: A separate Clinical Informatics subspecialty board examination exists. ABPM describes a current fellowship pathway; ABPath states that the certification is a joint and equal function of ABPath and ABPM, with ABPath diplomates applying/registering through ABPath and the examination administered through ABPM/Pearson VUE. This is distinct from the primary specialty board and not an institutional course exam.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: As checked 2026-10-07, ABPM’s current principal pathway requires successful completion of at least 24 months in an ACGME-accredited Clinical Informatics fellowship plus current primary specialty certification through an accepted board. ABPM’s general rules also include medical-degree and unrestricted-license requirements. ABPath diplomates use the ABPath application route; simultaneous pathology/CI training requires prior board/program approvals. Historical practice/non-accredited routes have cut-off dates and are not a current self-study pathway. Board rules can change; verify directly. This course, certificate, videos, or independent study confers no eligibility.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is a real physician subspecialty and the packet identifies two concrete Harvard-affiliated ACGME fellowship offerings. Boston Children’s has a pediatric-focused fellowship; BIDMC describes a general clinical informatics fellowship plus a distinct, approval-dependent ITE for non-pathology fellows with a research year. ABPath separately describes a simultaneous pathology route that is not claimed here as a BIDMC institutional track. Hopkins’s verified catalogue item is a multidisciplinary post-baccalaureate certificate, not a clinical physician fellowship. CHIP is a separate non-ACGME research programme. Institutional rotations, optional degrees, certificate courses, committee work, and online portal content are not equated with free public recorded lecture time. No claim is made that this packet exhausts every U.S. programme.
sourceCaveats: ABPM and ABPath pages were checked on 2026-10-07; they describe current fellowship-route eligibility and the separate exam. Historical pathways have board-specific deadlines and are not represented as open.

BIDMC’s current public page describes an ITE for non-pathology fellows with a research year and board-approval conditions; ABPath separately documents simultaneous pathology/CI training. Do not merge these distinct routes or infer an automatic dual-board outcome.
Boston Children’s public page says its fellowships are ACGME approved and describes pediatric focus; its public curriculum is not a complete lecture catalogue or a published didactic-hour schedule.
JHU’s 2026–27 catalogue entry is a post-baccalaureate certificate with a practicum; it is not an ACGME physician fellowship or ABPM eligibility substitute.
BCH’s separate CHIP research programme is explicitly not an ACGME-accredited fellowship.
Harvard Clinical Informatics Lecture Series requires Zoom registration linked to an active Zoom account; session length in a schedule is not observed free public video duration.
AMIA lists more than 32 hours in Health Informatics Essentials and 30 hours in CIBRC+ online; public free access to the individual videos was not established, so none counted.

MIT says its course combines Spring 2011 and Spring 2012 materials, and videos are from Spring 2011; only three existing direct-media ffprobe results were reusable. Other runtimes were unresolved and excluded. MIT videos are broad QI/health-systems foundation, not fellowship lectures.

The 2025 ACGME requirements PDF is linked but text extraction failed in this session; no granular requirement is quoted from that PDF. Program-level details were taken from institutions and current board pages.
Free-to-view educational cases are linked only; their content, images, and patient details are not copied or licensed by this course.

Clinical content and institutional programmes have not undergone human clinical review. This independent course is unaffiliated and does not replace medical school, ACGME training, licensure, supervised patient care, or board certification.

topicGaps: No public board-directed Clinical Informatics fellowship lecture catalogue with observed duration has been verified; the new recordings are broad health-informatics survey talks, not a substitute for ACGME clinical training or a complete ABPM/ABPath review course.

No observed lecture adequately covers the whole ABPM blueprint at board depth. Remaining thin/no-recording areas include detailed privacy/security and legal/ethical governance, full terminology and messaging standards beyond introductory FHIR, research versus transactional analytics, data-quality/stewardship and statistical validation, enterprise architecture/interoperability conformance, organizational budgeting/finance and leadership, implementation/maintenance, and rigorous clinical AI validation and monitoring.

The MIT and Paton recordings broaden systems, EHR/CPOE/CDS, workflow, usability, consumer informatics, AI, FHIR, and improvement exposure; they do not establish depth, currency, board alignment, physician competence, or equivalent coverage of all five blueprint domains.

No accessible complete on-demand recording set was found for Harvard Clinical Informatics Lecture Series; registration-based meetings remain excluded. Public AMIA course announcements were not counted because individual unrestricted lecture access and durations were not established.

21.2897 verified hours remain to the 36-hour target. Published course pages support further learning but not 21.29 hours of qualifying recordings; do not pad or relabel reading time, constructed episodes, or estimated media as verified hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: The ABPM Clinical Informatics Content Outline assigns what weight to “Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes”?
practiceQuestions.rationale: The published outline lists Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes as 30% of the exam content. This domain includes CDS, workflow, QI, usability, and outcome measurement.
practiceQuestions.domain: II. Improving Care Delivery and Outcomes

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional clinic reports that an alert reaches many staff members who cannot complete the follow-up task. Which CDS “right” is most directly implicated?

options.text: Right person
Right clinical answer is guaranteed
Right diagnosis code
Right vendor

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPM Five Rights include the right person; routing to a recipient who does not own or cannot act on the task is a role/workflow mismatch.

practiceQuestions.stem: A CDS alert is frequently overridden. What is the most defensible first interpretation?

options.text: The clinical rule is necessarily wrong.
The clinicians are necessarily unsafe.
The override rate is a signal to investigate alert relevance, workflow, and consequences.
All warnings should be removed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AHRQ describes alert fatigue and notes that high override rates can occur, but the rate alone does not establish cause. Investigate specificity, timing, workflow, and safety effects; do not automatically remove warnings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public health data exchange adopts FHIR. Which statement is best supported by the HL7 overview?

options.text: FHIR resources define exchangeable content, but implementation profiles and use cases still matter.
FHIR automatically resolves all terminology and identity mismatches.
FHIR is only a database schema and cannot be used with APIs.
FHIR makes governance and security unnecessary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HL7 describes resources as the basic building blocks and notes that use cases combine resources and can add profiles/constraints. The standard does not by itself remove semantic, identity, or governance work.

practiceQuestions.stem: Under the HIPAA Security Rule summary, which safeguard class is expressly included?

options.text: Only physical safeguards
Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards
Only encryption
A mandatory single vendor certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: HHS summarizes the Security Rule as requiring appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information; it is flexible and risk-based, not a single-vendor certification.
practiceQuestions.domain: I. Privacy, security, and legal/regulatory issues

practiceQuestions.stem: A team proposes using a single retrospective before/after percentage as proof that an EHR redesign caused an outcome improvement. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept causality because data are digital.
Reject all retrospective measurement.
Define measure provenance and consider confounding, secular trends, and balancing measures before making causal claims.
Replace outcome measures with login counts only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evaluation should define measures and data sources and consider alternative explanations and balancing effects. A simple before/after difference alone does not establish causal impact.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional risk model performs well on its development data, but the care setting and population change. What is the key informatics concern?

options.text: The model is automatically valid because it is unchanged.
Distribution shift and intended-use validity require evaluation and monitoring.
Calibration is irrelevant to clinical use.
The model should be deployed without governance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIST AI RMF emphasizes risk management across design, development, use, and evaluation. Generalization, intended use, and monitoring matter; development performance alone is insufficient.

practiceQuestions.stem: An EHR downtime exercise should most directly examine which capability?

options.text: How teams communicate and safely reconcile work/data when systems return.
How to bypass all access controls.
How to rely on memory instead of contingency plans.
How to suppress every alert permanently.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ONC’s 2025 SAFER Contingency Planning and System Management guides address safe practices for unavailable systems, resilience, and technical operations. Downtime planning should include communication and reconciliation.
practiceQuestions.domain: III. Enterprise systems and downtime mitigation

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes current Clinical Informatics subspecialty certification eligibility as of the date checked?

options.text: Any online course completion grants eligibility.
The current main path requires at least 24 months of ACGME-accredited CI fellowship and current primary board certification, subject to the board’s full rules.
A Johns Hopkins post-baccalaureate certificate alone qualifies for the subspecialty exam.
No separate Clinical Informatics exam exists.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPM’s current published fellowship pathway requires completion of a 24-month ACGME-accredited Clinical Informatics fellowship plus current primary specialty board certification. The certificate and independent study do not substitute. ABPath diplomates apply through ABPath for the joint/equal subspecialty exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: A software team asks whether a recommendation feature is automatically “non-device CDS.” What is the safest informatics answer?

options.text: Yes, every clinician-facing recommendation is exempt.
No; assess the actual software function and intended use against current FDA guidance, and consult qualified regulatory expertise.
Yes, if a physician is involved.
No clinical software is ever exempt.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA’s January 2026 guidance explains its interpretation of statutory criteria for certain non-device CDS functions and continues to apply policies to functions meeting the device definition. Specific status depends on facts and intended use.

title: Complex Care Fellowship
level: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship-aligned independent study

prerequisites.suggestedLearnerLevel: Physicians in or after pediatrics or medicine-pediatrics training and interprofessional learners who can interpret pediatric clinical literature. It is also suitable for educators/health-services learners with appropriate supervision.
knowledgePrerequisites: Pediatric history, physical examination, pharmacology, and common chronic-condition foundations.
Ability to appraise guidelines and communicate uncertainty.
Local supervised training before any device care, emergency response, order writing, procedure, or patient-specific decision.
prerequisites.officialApplicationBoundary: Boston Children’s public application page currently requests a letter of intent, CV, and three references (including one from the residency program director). That page does not publish a separate ABP eligibility pathway; do not treat these application materials as a board requirement.

objectives: Characterize medical complexity with function, technology, utilization, family priorities, social context, and care network.
Apply published complex-care EPA themes to care planning, feeding/aspiration, technology safety, care coordination, transition, advocacy, and goals-of-care discussions.
Use family-centered, disability-affirming communication and closed-loop cross-setting coordination.
Translate current home-health and tracheostomy guideline recommendations into questions for supervised local care planning without giving remote patient-specific orders.
Critically appraise complex-care evidence and design ethical QI/scholarly work without using real patient records.
State the exact accreditation, board, and clinical-training boundaries of independent study.

units.title: Recognizing medical complexity and building a longitudinal assessment
objectives: Differentiate CMC from the broader CYSHCN population using the AAP description rather than diagnosis count alone.
Synthesize conditions, function, technology, medications, utilization, family capacity, social context, and goals into a problem representation.
Prioritize a longitudinal care-plan problem list and identify acute-change red flags that need an escalation pathway.
boardDomains: Educational CMC EPA alignment: common clinical issues; not an ABP Complex Care exam domain
units.casePractice: Use a fictional composite with neurodisability, enteral feeding, and recurrent admissions to write a one-page problem representation; do not use a real chart.
units.assessment: Faculty/self-review rubric: accuracy of CMC characterization, function/technology capture, family goals, and uncertainty identification.

units.title: Feeding, aspiration, nutrition, pain, and neuromusculoskeletal care
objectives: Frame feeding difficulty, aspiration risk, pain/irritability, growth, and abnormal tone as linked but separately assessed problems.
Name the relevant complex-care EPAs and identify when multidisciplinary evaluation is needed.
Interpret a linked authentic teaching image only in its original source context, with no claim that one image establishes a diagnosis.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPAs: feeding/nutritional concerns; routine feeding-tube care; pain/irritability; aspiration; common neuromuscular/skeletal issues
units.casePractice: Linked-only image appraisal: Open-i result “Right Angle Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Tube Extension to Prevent Tube-Induced Jejunoduodenal Intussusception,” Figure 1. It is an authentic published CT figure. Read its source article and its license before any reuse; use only for image-literacy discussion, not a procedural simulation.
units.assessment: Short answer: distinguish a symptom, a feeding-device issue, and a need for urgent clinical assessment; cite evidence limits.

units.title: Family partnership, communication, disability justice, and shared decisions
objectives: Use family-centered, accessible, language-concordant communication and define team roles with families.
Separate shared decision-making from mere information delivery and elicit what matters to the child and family.
Recognize disability discrimination and structural barriers as care-quality issues, not family deficits.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPAs: care coordination, goals of care, advocacy; ABP EPA educational framework only
units.casePractice: Role-play with a fictional family: revise a jargon-heavy discharge message into a teach-back-ready plan while preserving uncertainty and interpreter needs.
units.assessment: Observed structured communication exercise; assess agenda setting, teach-back, family goals, role clarity, and avoidance of deficit language.

units.title: Technology dependence, emergency planning, and home safety
objectives: Create a technology inventory that connects device, supply, caregiver competency, emergency plan, and responsible clinician.
Apply the 2025 ATS tracheostomy recommendations conceptually; distinguish a guideline recommendation from an individual order.
Design a safety/emergency plan and identify the limits of telemonitoring and of independent-study procedural learning.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPAs: routine technology care/troubleshooting; safety/emergency plans
units.casePractice: Fictional tabletop: identify missing elements in a home emergency plan for a child with a tracheostomy and feeding tube. No hands-on tracheostomy or device procedure is taught or authorized.
units.assessment: Checklist scored against identified risks, family training, supplies, escalation contacts, and site-specific emergency resources.

units.title: Care across inpatient, perioperative, post-acute, and home settings
objectives: Reconcile a care plan across admission, procedure, discharge, primary care, specialty care, post-acute care, and home.
Identify minimum handoff information and confirm medication, equipment, follow-up, and caregiver readiness before a fictional discharge.
Explain why a clinical rotation cannot be converted into self-study lecture hours.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPA alignment: common clinical issues, technology, care coordination, safety; no Complex Care board domain
units.casePractice: Fictional discharge huddle: create a written handoff with accurate medication reconciliation placeholders, supply confirmation, named follow-up roles, and contingency instructions.
units.assessment: Discharge-plan audit; no clinical sign-off or procedure credit.

units.title: Ethics, palliative care, and goals-of-care conversations
objectives: Describe the overlapping but distinct roles of complex care and palliative care without assuming a prognosis.
Prepare for a values-based goals-of-care conversation using shared decision-making and appropriate uncertainty.
Identify ethical conflicts around interventions, feeding, surgery, and caregiver burden and seek supervised ethics/palliative support when needed.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPA: facilitate goals-of-care discussions and introduce palliative/hospice concepts
units.casePractice: Fictional family-meeting preparation: develop neutral questions, a values summary, and a plan for interpreter and palliative/ethics involvement. Do not write a treatment recommendation.
units.assessment: Structured note is assessed for neutrality, values elicitation, role clarity, and explicit uncertainty.

units.title: Mental health, social needs, access, and equity
objectives: Screen for social needs and mental-health concerns as part of a whole-family CMC assessment.
Map access barriers across geography, insurance, language, school, transport, and home-nursing workforce without assigning blame.
Plan a closed-loop referral and follow-up process for a fictional scenario.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPA alignment: advocacy and care coordination
units.casePractice: Fictional resource map: choose culturally and linguistically appropriate supports and specify who confirms uptake; do not promise service availability.
units.assessment: Equity-focused care-coordination plan rated for feasibility, family input, and closed-loop follow-up.

units.title: Medical home, care coordination, advocacy, and system design
objectives: Distinguish care coordination from disease or agency-limited case management.
Map responsibilities between primary care, specialty teams, school, home health, payer, and family.
Apply advocacy principles to equipment, nursing, school, and service barriers while respecting local law and coverage variation.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPAs: team-based care coordination; advocacy for CMC/families
units.casePractice: Fictional systems map: document accountable roles and bidirectional communication routes; no billing or legal advice.
units.assessment: Care-map rubric: named owners, data sharing, contingency, family authority, and equity check.

units.title: Transition to adult-oriented care and life-course planning
objectives: Use the Six Core Elements to organize a transition process rather than treating transfer as a single referral.
Identify readiness, guardianship/consent questions, equipment, benefits, and adult-clinician continuity as separate planning workstreams.
Plan sequential transfer of multiple specialty relationships in a fictional CMC case.
boardDomains: Published CMC EPA: developmentally appropriate transition process to adult care
units.casePractice: Fictional 17-year-old transition bundle: readiness assessment, portable medical summary outline, transfer checklist, and confirmation step.
units.assessment: Six-Core-Elements checklist; no assertion that a plan establishes adult-service eligibility.

units.title: Evidence, quality improvement, scholarship, and outcomes
objectives: Critically appraise a complex-care study for population, outcome choice, family partnership, bias, and implementation context.
Create a feasible QI aim and measure set without promising utilization or cost outcomes.
Differentiate scholarly activity from an independent study artifact and recognize that Boston Children’s expects mentored scholarship in its actual fellowship.
boardDomains: BCH scholarship expectation; educational framework, not board examination content
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional QI charter to improve completeness of a care-plan field; do not use patient data or submit it as human-subjects research.
units.assessment: Appraisal worksheet and QI charter reviewed for outcome validity, equity, data governance, and limits.

units.title: Teaching, leadership, and integrated capstone
objectives: Teach a short CMC case using source attribution, transparency about uncertainty, and psychologically safe discussion.
Integrate assessment, coordination, safety, equity, transition, and scholarship into a longitudinal fictional case plan.
State the limits of independent study and when clinical supervision, local policy, or specialist input is required.
boardDomains: BCH teaching/leadership opportunities; not an ABP Complex Care board blueprint
units.casePractice: Present a fictional composite case with a source-backed care map, safety plan, transition screen, and an evidence gap statement.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric plus self-reflection; independent-study completion only.

assignment.title: Fictional longitudinal complex-care portfolio
components: A one-page fictional composite problem representation and family-priority statement.
A cross-setting care map with accountable roles, communication routes, language access, and closed-loop follow-up.
A fictional technology/safety plan that cites the ATS and AAP sources but does not give a procedural protocol.
A Six Core Elements transition screen or a goals-of-care meeting preparation note.
A 500–750-word evidence/QI reflection using no patient data.
assignment.restriction: Use only fictional composites, publicly licensed teaching images linked to their source, or local institution-approved simulations. Do not upload real patient records, identifying information, protected images, or clinical orders.

formative: Unit retrieval questions and reflection prompts.
Structured communication/teach-back simulation using fictional cases.
summative: Ten original source-cited practice questions in this entry.
Portfolio rubric: clinical reasoning 25%, family partnership/equity 25%, safety and cross-setting coordination 25%, evidence/limitations and source attribution 25%.
assessment.passingBoundary: No grade, completion badge, or portfolio result establishes competency, certification, fellowship credit, clinical privileges, board eligibility, licensure, or predicted examination performance.

studyHours.basis: Transparent independent-study plan: only 18.705278 externally verified ready video hours count now. The 17.3 original-video plan is not rendered and is excluded from verified hours. Remaining time is reading, linked case appraisal, fictional simulation, assignments, and reflection; it is not clinical rotation time.

mapping.name: Complex Care Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Actual separate two-year fellowship for pediatricians, not a generic directory category. Boston Children’s publishes broad clinical exposure across primary-care medical home, consultative coordination, multidisciplinary clinics, perioperative/inpatient/palliative/urgent/home/telehealth/post-acute/skilled-nursing settings; longitudinal panel care; Rainbow, Complex Care Service, CP/Spasticity, Spina Bifida, Aerodigestive, and Craniofacial programs; EPA-oriented assessment; seminars/case discussions/journal clubs; and a mentored scholarly project. Public pages do not disclose a complete lecture catalogue or enough official lecture duration to count 36 hours.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 7-year-old with cerebral palsy, gastrostomy dependence, chronic lung disease, mobility limitations, and recurrent admissions is being assessed in a complex-care clinic. Which feature best supports describing the child as having medical complexity under the AAP framework?

options.text: Use of more than three medications alone
The combination of multiple significant chronic problems, functional limitation, high need/use, and possible technology assistance
Any single rare diagnosis
Only the annual cost of care

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP describes CMC through interacting chronic problems, functional limitations, high health-care need/use, and often technology assistance—not a medication count, rarity, or cost alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional discharge planning meeting, a hospital case manager can arrange services only covered by that agency. The complex-care clinician is asked to coordinate school, home health, specialists, and the family’s stated priorities. What best distinguishes the latter work?

options.text: It is limited to ordering tests
It is care coordination: a team-based, patient- and family-centered process across people and systems
It replaces the family’s role in decisions
It means one clinician must provide every service

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP policy distinguishes broader patient- and family-centered care coordination from agency-limited disease/case management and emphasizes cross-system work with families.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional parent says that a home-care instruction is difficult to understand. Which response best uses teach-back?

options.text: Ask the parent to sign that the instructions were received
Repeat the same technical wording more slowly
Ask how the parent would explain the plan to the evening caregiver, then clarify gaps
Ask a sibling to interpret

practiceQuestions.rationale: Teach-back checks the clarity of the team’s explanation and supports a patient/family-centered plan. It is not a test of the family, and a qualified interpreter is needed when appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child with a tracheostomy is at risk of immediate decompensation from tracheostomy-related complications. According to the 2025 ATS guideline, which general safety principle is recommended?

options.text: Routine tracheal cultures in every well child
An awake and alert trained caregiver should always be present
Telemonitoring replaces trained caregivers
All children need the same discharge process regardless of risk

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ATS recommends an awake and alert trained caregiver for children at risk of immediate decompensation. It suggests against routine surveillance cultures in well children and notes that telemonitoring does not replace skilled care. Individual plans still require local/supervised clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which item is the most appropriate element of a fictional cross-setting discharge plan for a child with complex medical needs?

options.text: A discharge summary only, sent after the first outpatient visit
A jointly developed, accessible plan with medication/equipment details, identified contacts, and direct communication with the primary clinician
A statement that the parent is solely responsible for coordinating all specialists
A generic online handout with no local contact information

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 AAP home-health report emphasizes communication with the primary clinician, confirmation of medications/supplies, and an immediately accessible care plan jointly developed with family, medical team, and coordinators.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 17-year-old with medical complexity is preparing to move to adult-oriented care. Which set matches the pediatric-practice version of the Six Core Elements?

options.text: Policy, tracking/monitoring, readiness assessment, transition planning, transfer, and transfer completion
Diagnosis, procedure, prescription, billing, discharge, and audit
Referral, appointment, transfer, discharge, closure, and readmission
Guardianship, insurance, equipment, housing, college, and employment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP report identifies policy, tracking/monitoring, readiness, planning, transfer, and completion for pediatric practices. The other issues can matter but are not the named six elements.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which activity is one of the published complex-care EPAs described in the literature?

options.text: Independently credentialing clinicians for invasive procedures
Facilitating team-based care coordination for children with medical complexity
Passing a separate ABP Complex Care certification examination
Replacing all subspecialist assessments

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published framework includes team-based care coordination. EPAs are educational activities; they neither credential procedures nor create an ABP Complex Care examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional family is uncertain whether to pursue a burdensome intervention. What is the best initial complex-care action?

options.text: Assume palliative care is appropriate only when all treatment stops
Promise that a single option is objectively best
Elicit values and goals, communicate uncertainty, and involve supervised palliative/ethics support when appropriate
Delay discussion until an emergency occurs

practiceQuestions.rationale: The complex-care EPA framework includes facilitating goals-of-care discussions and introducing palliative/hospice concepts. This calls for shared decision-making and support, not prognostic assumptions or unsupervised treatment advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child’s home-nursing coverage is unreliable because of workforce shortages. Which plan best reflects equity-focused care coordination?

options.text: Document that the family declined services
Treat missed nursing as a family adherence problem
Discuss risks and mitigation with the family, identify accountable team follow-up, and advocate within local service/payer systems without promising availability
Use telemonitoring as a complete substitute for caregivers

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP home-health report addresses workforce and equity barriers; ATS guidance notes telemonitoring cannot replace skilled care. A transparent, closed-loop plan avoids blaming families and avoids promises outside the team’s control.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the certification boundary for this course and the declared Boston Children’s Complex Care Fellowship?

options.text: Completion automatically grants ABP Complex Care certification
The programme is an ACGME pediatric subspecialty with a published ABP Complex Care board blueprint
Complex Care is not listed as an ABP certificate or ACGME Pediatrics subspecialty; this independent course cannot confer eligibility, licensure, or fellowship credit
Any two-year fellowship is interchangeable with an ABP-recognized subspecialty fellowship

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current ABP certificate portal and ACGME Pediatrics subspecialty list do not name Complex Care. ABP’s recognized-subspecialty criteria require specific training verification. The declared item packet categorizes the Boston fellowship as non-ACGME, and its independent-study counterpart confers no credential.

title: Family Medicine Master Teacher Fellowship
level: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship; medical-education faculty-development track-aligned independent study

prerequisites.intendedLearner: Family medicine physicians, senior residents, or clinician-educators who want a rigorous educational-design curriculum. The actual CHA fellowship publicly limits eligibility to family medicine physicians licensed or eligible for Massachusetts medical licensure.
independentStudyMinimum: Ability to read clinical/education literature and use a public web-video player.
A fictional or locally authorized teaching context; independent learners must not use patient records, learner records, protected images, or local quality data in this course.
For any real clinical teaching, research, assessment, or data use: local appointment/privileges, supervision, privacy compliance, consent, and ethics/IRB review where applicable.
notPrerequisitesOrPermissions: This course does not require or create CHA affiliation, Massachusetts licensure, clinical privileges, a faculty appointment, permission to precept, IRB approval, ABFM eligibility, CAQ eligibility, or certification.

objectives: State the actual scope and limits of the CHA Master Teacher Fellowship and this independent course.
Write observable objectives aligned to active-learning activities and assessments.
Teach clinical reasoning and information mastery without converting evidence review into unsupervised clinical advice.
Plan supervised outpatient/bedside teaching with a patient-safety and privacy boundary.
Use formative coaching and feedback that is specific, equitable, and psychologically safer.
Design a competency-based curriculum map and an accessible virtual-learning element.
Develop an assessment plan with an intended-use statement, validity-evidence plan, and fairness check.
Critically appraise evidence and translate it into cautious teaching claims.
Plan an ethical evaluation or education-scholarship project with appropriate local review.
Build a teaching portfolio, mentoring, and dissemination plan.

units.title: Programme identity, scope, and the clinician-educator role
objectives: Distinguish CHA’s actual two-year full-time onsite faculty-development fellowship from Family Medicine residency, a generic directory category, or a clinical subspecialty fellowship.
Set an educator role statement that separates local clinical privileges and supervision from independent study.
boardDomains: No separate fellowship blueprint or exam exists. Context only: ABFM Foundations of Care (professionalism, systems, health equity).
units.casePractice: Create a de-identified fictional scenario about an outpatient learner needing coaching; do not use patient data.
units.assessment: 250-word role-and-scope statement with a boundary checklist.

units.title: Adult learning, cognitive load, and active learning
objectives: Select an active-learning method that follows from a measurable objective and learner level.
Revise a slide or short teaching segment to reduce extraneous cognitive load while preserving clinical reasoning.
boardDomains: Educator application across all five ABFM clinical domains; not clinical-content preparation.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional hypertension follow-up vignette only to prototype a pause-and-predict activity; no management answer is assessed.
units.assessment: Submit an objective, a 10-minute activity, and a brief cognitive-load rationale.

units.title: Teaching clinical reasoning and information mastery
objectives: Teach a learner to articulate a problem representation, prioritized differential, and uncertainty.
Model question formulation and appraisal rather than presenting an unsupported authority conclusion.
boardDomains: ABFM Acute Care and Diagnosis (35%) and Foundations of Care (statistics); used only as a contextual map.
units.casePractice: Link-only discussion of a published CC BY case-report education resource; make a teaching plan, not a patient-specific recommendation.
units.assessment: Observed 5-minute think-aloud teaching demonstration, peer rubric, and self-reflection.

units.title: Outpatient precepting, bedside teaching, and graded supervision
objectives: Design a precepting encounter that makes learner reasoning observable while preserving patient safety and consent.
Specify what must be supervised locally and what can be practised in simulation or with fictional cases.
boardDomains: ABFM Acute, Chronic, Preventive, Emergent/Urgent, and Foundations domains as settings learners may encounter; this unit does not certify competence in them.
units.casePractice: Plan a supervised teaching encounter using a fictional chronic-disease follow-up; no real clinic or patient participation is part of this course.
units.assessment: Precepting plan with learning objective, supervision trigger, feedback plan, and patient-safety stop rule.

units.title: Coaching, feedback, and psychologically safer learning
objectives: Give behaviorally specific feedback tied to a directly observed task and invite learner response.
Identify a change that can make learner assessment and feedback more equitable and psychologically safer.
boardDomains: ABFM Foundations of Care context: communication, equity, legal/professional issues.
units.casePractice: Use an original fictional feedback conversation; never publish an identifiable learner evaluation.
units.assessment: Audio-free written feedback script plus learner self-assessment prompt and privacy review.

units.title: Competency-based design, objectives, and virtual learning
objectives: Write observable objectives aligned to an activity, assessment, and evidence of achievement.
Choose a virtual-learning approach appropriate to access, privacy, accessibility, and a local approval process.
boardDomains: ABFM Foundations of Care context; ACGME/ABFM competency documents are residency-program resources, not a fellowship exam blueprint.
units.casePractice: Build an asynchronous fictional case discussion with no real image, EHR capture, or protected data.
units.assessment: Objective–activity–assessment alignment matrix and an accessibility/privacy note.

units.title: Curriculum planning and program-level change
objectives: Conduct a narrow learner/environment needs assessment and define an achievable curriculum aim.
Map a session sequence to objectives, delivery method, assessment, and revision signal.
boardDomains: All five ABFM care domains may inform a locally chosen clinical content area; no ABFM content coverage is claimed.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional clinic teaching problem (late follow-up documentation) to construct a curriculum map; it is not a quality-improvement intervention.
units.assessment: One-page curriculum map and feasibility/risk review.

units.title: Assessment, fairness, and validity evidence
objectives: Differentiate formative coaching from a high-stakes decision.
Frame validity as evidence supporting an intended score interpretation and use, not an inherent property of an instrument.
Identify a potential fairness threat and a data source for monitoring it.
boardDomains: ABFM Foundations of Care (statistics, legal issues, health equity) contextual mapping only.
units.casePractice: Audit a fictional mini-CEX form for unclear anchors and potential bias; do not use an actual learner record.
units.assessment: Assessment blueprint, intended-use statement, and validity/fairness evidence plan.

units.title: Critical appraisal and evidence-to-teaching translation
objectives: Construct a focused clinical or educational question and locate an appropriate evidence source.
Explain how study design, effect estimates, uncertainty, and applicability constrain a teaching claim.
topics: critical appraisal of therapy and diagnosis
sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios
boardDomains: ABFM Foundations of Care (statistics) and Acute/Chronic care teaching context; not an exam review.
units.casePractice: Use the linked CC BY case-report education article only as a prompt to plan an appraisal discussion; no patient data or images may be copied.
units.assessment: One-page evidence appraisal and a two-question learner check.

units.title: Health equity, social context, and inclusive curriculum
objectives: Identify where social context and structural barriers alter a curriculum’s case framing or assessment opportunity.
Revise a teaching case to avoid stigmatizing assumptions while retaining diagnostic uncertainty.
boardDomains: ABFM Foundations of Care (health equity) and Preventive Care context; no clinical guideline recommendations are taught.
units.casePractice: Use original fictional cases with deliberately non-identifying, non-stereotyped details; do not alter a real patient narrative.
units.assessment: Equity review of a case prompt and a rationale for revisions.

units.title: Education research, evaluation, and scholarship
objectives: Distinguish evaluation for local improvement from research intended to generate generalizable knowledge.
Select a feasible question, outcome, method, and dissemination route while recognizing when local IRB/ethics review is required.
boardDomains: No clinical board-content claim; ABFM Foundations of Care context for statistics and systems.
units.casePractice: Use a synthetic aggregate course-evaluation dataset; never upload learner records or patient data.
units.assessment: Protocol synopsis: question, stakeholders, data minimization, ethics/IRB question, analysis, dissemination.

units.title: Leadership, mentoring, portfolio, and dissemination
objectives: Build a teaching portfolio that documents contribution, reflection, and evidence without exposing learner or patient information.
Develop a mentoring and dissemination plan with authorship, conflict-of-interest, and accessibility considerations.
boardDomains: No fellowship board blueprint. ABFM Foundations of Care is a contextual—not qualifying—reference.
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional abstract/presentation plan from a synthetic evaluation; no real outcomes or identifiable quotes.
units.assessment: Portfolio excerpt, dissemination abstract, and mentor feedback plan.

assignment.title: Capstone: a bounded, evidence-informed family-medicine teaching innovation
deliverables: One-page needs/scope statement and observable objectives.
Curriculum map with one active-learning activity and assessment alignment.
A fictional or locally authorized case-discussion plan; no real patient record, image, learner record, or protected data.
Feedback/coaching script and privacy/equity check.
Assessment blueprint, intended score-use statement, and validity/fairness evidence plan.
Two-page evaluation or scholarship synopsis that states whether local ethics/IRB consultation is needed.
Teaching-portfolio excerpt and dissemination abstract.
assignment.submissionBoundary: This independent course does not collect submissions, grade clinical competence, approve research, or authorize implementation. Use a locally qualified educator/ethics process for any actual deployment.

formative: Five-minute teaching demonstration using a fictional scenario.
assessment.summativePlan: Self-assessed capstone portfolio using a transparent rubric: scope and safety 20%, instructional alignment 20%, reasoning/evidence quality 20%, assessment/validity/equity 20%, evaluation/scholarship/communication 20%. This is an educational self-assessment, not an official CHA, ACGME, ABFM, or licensing assessment.
assessment.passingBoundary: No pass, credential, CME, academic credit, clinical competency determination, or board-readiness claim is issued.

studyHours.type: transparent independent-study plan; not a representation of CHA fellowship time
studyHours.note: Only verified ready recordings contribute to verifiedExternalHours. Planned original clips are neither ready nor counted.

mapping.name: Family Medicine Master Teacher Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA describes a two-year, full-time onsite faculty-development programme for medical educators. It integrates a University of Dundee distance-learning Master’s in Medical Education, maintains clinical practice at CHA Malden Care Center, allocates approximately 30% time to clinical practice, and uses the balance for teaching and learning. CHA says clinical teaching starts with supervision and then becomes independent precepting; fellows may deliver lectures/small groups. These are actual fellowship activities, not independent-course lectures.

medical.boardStatus: No separate ABFM/ABMS board examination, Certificate of Added Qualification, or board-eligibility pathway for “Family Medicine Master Teacher Fellowship” was identified in CHA or ABFM public sources. medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABFM states that Family Medicine board eligibility begins the day after successful completion of an ACGME-accredited Family Medicine residency and expires December 31 of the seventh calendar year after completion, subject to ABFM requirements. CHA’s public fellowship page requires Family Medicine physicians licensed or eligible for Massachusetts medical licensure; it does not say fellowship completion creates or extends ABFM eligibility. ABFM’s current CAQs are Adolescent Medicine, Geriatric Medicine, Hospice and Palliative Medicine, Pain Medicine, Sleep Medicine, Sports Medicine, and Health Care Administration, Leadership, and Management; medical education/master teaching is not listed. This independent study confers none of the foregoing.

officialProgrammes.name: Family Medicine Master Teacher Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA describes a two-year, full-time onsite faculty-development programme for medical educators. It integrates a University of Dundee distance-learning Master’s in Medical Education, maintains clinical practice at CHA Malden Care Center, allocates approximately 30% time to clinical practice, and uses the balance for teaching and learning. CHA says clinical teaching starts with supervision and then becomes independent precepting; fellows may deliver lectures/small groups. These are actual fellowship activities, not independent-course lectures.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This independent curriculum studies the public CHA programme’s educator-development themes: teaching and learning, curriculum planning, assessment, leadership/management, medical-education research, information mastery, virtual learning, and supervised clinical teaching. It does not reproduce or claim access to CHA’s proprietary Dundee coursework, seminars, clinical patient panel, inpatient teaching, precepting, employment, or evaluation.
sourceCaveats: All institutional webpages, ABFM/ACGME sources, and public video metadata were checked on 2026-10-07. Policies, eligibility, archive access, and programme details can change; re-check before relying on them.

CHA’s published page confirms an actual fellowship but does not establish ACGME accreditation, a separate ABMS specialty, a board examination, formal didactic-hour total, lecture catalogue, procedure/case minimums, or a clinical rotation schedule. None is inferred.
The University of Dundee degree/coursework is mentioned by CHA, but no proprietary Dundee assignments, recordings, tuition, enrollment, or credential is supplied by this course.
The 42 FAME recordings are external Northwestern faculty-development content. They are not claimed to be CHA lectures, required by CHA, CME, or reusable media.

The user-supplied nuclear-medicine/radiology outline concerns a different subject. Its clinical, imaging, tracer, volume, and certification claims were not imported into this family-medicine educator course.
No practice question uses proprietary or leaked exam material. No original planned clip is counted until produced, publicly hosted, and duration-verified.

This is independent self-study, unaffiliated with CHA, ABFM, ACGME, Northwestern, or University of Dundee. It is not MD/DO education, residency/fellowship completion, clinical credentialing, licensure, board eligibility/certification, CME, or a guarantee of passing any exam.
