practiceQuestions.stem: A faculty member writes: “Learners will understand safe outpatient precepting.” Which revision is most assessable?

options.text: Learners will appreciate the complexity of precepting.
Learners will list three patient-safety triggers that require direct faculty supervision during a precepting encounter.
Learners will know when to precept.
Learners will be exposed to supervision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: “List three … triggers” specifies an observable performance and can be aligned with an activity and assessment. The other verbs do not establish an observable standard.
practiceQuestions.domain: Unit 6—competency-based design; contextual ABFM Foundations of Care

practiceQuestions.stem: During a case presentation, a resident omits a key negative finding. The preceptor wants formative feedback. What is the best first move?

options.text: Record a failing summative score without discussion.
State a directly observed behavior, ask the resident to self-assess, and agree on one specific next step.
Correct the resident publicly and provide no opportunity to respond.
Wait until the end of the rotation and give a global impression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evidence-informed feedback should be timely, behaviorally anchored, interactive, and oriented to a feasible improvement action.

practiceQuestions.stem: A program uses the same oral-presentation rubric for early students and senior residents. Which statement about validity is most accurate?

options.text: The rubric is permanently valid because faculty wrote it.
Validity concerns the appropriateness of score interpretations and uses in a specified context, supported by accumulating evidence.
A high average score proves validity.
Reliability alone establishes validity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Modern validity theory evaluates inferences and intended uses, not a fixed property of an instrument; evidence is contextual and ongoing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A faculty member wants to teach information mastery from a newly published single-center study. What should learners do before changing a teaching claim into a clinical recommendation?

options.text: Adopt the conclusion because the result is recent.
Assess the clinical question, design, results/uncertainty, applicability, and relevant guidelines or higher-level evidence.
Use the abstract only to save time.
Use the presenter’s specialty as the main credibility test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evidence-based practice integrates evidence with clinical expertise and requires critical assessment of research and guidelines; recency or authority alone is insufficient.
practiceQuestions.domain: Unit 9—information mastery; contextual ABFM Foundations of Care

practiceQuestions.stem: A proposed online case conference requires screenshots from a real patient’s portal to make it realistic. What is the correct course-design decision?

options.text: Use the screenshots if names are cropped.
Upload them to a private class drive because learners are clinicians.
Do not use them in this independent course; use a fictional/de-identified lawful resource and obtain local approvals for any clinical teaching use.
Use them after telling learners not to share.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This independent curriculum has no authority to use patient records. Removing a name alone does not establish lawful de-identification, consent, or local approval.
practiceQuestions.domain: Unit 4/6—clinical teaching boundaries and virtual learning

practiceQuestions.stem: A course director wants to decide whether feedback training reduced bias in narrative evaluations. Which plan best separates evaluation from a high-stakes claim?

options.text: Announce that the intervention eliminated bias after two comments.
Define the intended local use, collect only necessary aggregate data, examine alternative explanations and fairness, and seek local ethics/IRB guidance before generalizable research.
Publish raw learner comments with names removed.
Skip data collection because feedback is inherently beneficial.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Program evaluation needs a defined use and appropriate data; broader research and data sharing may raise ethics/IRB issues. Fairness conclusions require evidence, not assertion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A curriculum is mapped to a local ambulatory diabetes case, but the instructor says it guarantees ABFM certification. Which correction is required?

options.text: The guarantee is appropriate if the case is high quality.
Rename the course a fellowship examination preparation course.
State that ABFM’s clinical blueprint can contextualize family-medicine content, but this educator curriculum is not ABFM preparation, certification, or eligibility training.
Remove all objectives.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABFM blueprint describes clinical examination content. CHA’s program is an educator fellowship, and no separate master-teacher board examination or eligibility path was identified.

practiceQuestions.stem: A faculty member asks whether clinical time in the actual CHA fellowship should be counted as this course’s lecture time. What is correct?

options.text: Yes, any patient-care hour equals a lecture hour.
Yes, if it occurs on a Tuesday or Thursday.
No. CHA describes clinical practice/precepting as fellowship activity; only observed-duration, accessible recordings count toward this independent course’s video total.
Only inpatient teaching counts as a lecture.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CHA page describes approximately 30% clinical practice and precepting. This ledger counts only unique accessible recordings with observed durations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner designs a survey after a workshop and intends to claim that the workshop improved clinical competence. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Treat satisfaction as direct proof of competence.
Specify the competence inference, choose an aligned outcome and evidence plan, and report the limits of the survey.
Report only favorable comments.
Call the survey a validated instrument without evidence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A satisfaction survey may be useful for a narrow purpose, but it cannot by itself support a broad competence inference. Validity evidence must match the claim and use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A new teacher notices that a case depicts a patient as “noncompliant” without context. Which revision best supports equitable teaching?

options.text: Keep the label because it is shorter.
Replace it with neutral, specific information about what occurred and invite consideration of access, communication, preferences, and structural barriers without assuming cause.
Delete all social context from every case.
Assign the same explanation to all patients with missed visits.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Specific non-stigmatizing language and attention to context prevent unsupported assumptions. The aim is not to erase social context but to frame it carefully.

title: Family Medicine Residency
prerequisites: For meaningful postgraduate-level study: foundational anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pathophysiology, clinical interviewing, physical-exam concepts, epidemiology, and biostatistics.
Ability to read current clinical guidance critically and identify population, date, caveats, and local-practice constraints.
No patient-care role is required or implied. Learners must not use real patient records, conduct procedures, or act beyond their authorization.
objectives: Map broad family medicine work to ABFM’s five published clinical-activity domains without claiming examination readiness.
Interpret prevention, chronic disease, acute-care, behavioral-health, pediatric, reproductive, older-adult, and health-system questions using current primary sources.
Separate clinical rotations, supervised procedures, licensing/certification standards, and board eligibility from independent video study.
Use accessible public recordings with their dates and limitations visible; replace dated advice with current primary guidance.
Practice evidence appraisal, safety-net reasoning, team-based care, equity-aware QI, and referral/escalation concepts through fictional cases.
Use authentic image resources only under their individual licenses and de-identification/redistribution conditions.

units.title: Scope, continuity, and evidence-based primary care
objectives: Explain longitudinal, relationship-based primary care and continuity-panel reasoning.
Frame a clinical question, locate an authoritative source, and state how evidence changes a care plan.
Differentiate a residency’s supervised clinical curriculum from this independent study sequence.
topics: Family medicine practice as educational foundation
units.casePractice: Write a PICO-style question from a fictional continuity-panel vignette; identify one guideline and one implementation limitation. Do not use patient records.
units.assessment: One-page evidence appraisal and a 10-item simulated panel-maintenance audit.

units.title: Prevention, screening, immunization, and counseling
objectives: Apply current preventive-service recommendations by patient context rather than memorized, static age lists.
Use current CDC schedule pages and contraindication/precaution resources rather than an archived lecture for vaccine decisions.
Communicate risk and uncertainty without coercion.
units.casePractice: Use a wholly fictional age/medical-history profile to locate, cite, and explain a current preventive recommendation. Do not create an individualized treatment plan.
units.assessment: Open-resource prevention matrix with citation and currency checks.

units.title: Adult chronic disease and multimorbidity
objectives: Prioritize competing chronic conditions and functional goals in a fictional longitudinal visit.
Recognize when a source requires current rechecking before clinical use.
Plan monitoring, referral, and follow-up concepts across diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, and kidney disease.
units.casePractice: Build a problem list and follow-up questions for a fictional adult with diabetes, hypertension, and reduced kidney function; identify information that would require verification.
units.assessment: Structured longitudinal-care reasoning note; no medication dose calculation.

units.title: Behavioral health, chronic pain, and substance use
objectives: Distinguish screening from diagnosis and connect a positive screen to systems for assessment, treatment, and follow-up.
Use person-centered, function-oriented chronic-pain reasoning.
State the limits of the 2022 CDC opioid guideline and avoid rigid or abrupt-taper interpretations.
units.casePractice: Discuss a fictional patient’s functional goals and safety questions with a standardized written script; do not prescribe, taper, or counsel a real person.
units.assessment: Closed-book safety/limits quiz plus reflective communication checklist.

units.title: Children, adolescents, and developmental care
objectives: Separate developmental monitoring, surveillance, validated screening, referral, and follow-up.
Organize anticipatory guidance across well-child care, adolescent confidentiality, and complex-care coordination.
Recognize when urgent symptoms or safeguarding concerns require supervised local escalation.
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional well-child workflows, marking where monitoring is not a substitute for validated screening and where referral follow-through is needed.
units.assessment: Pediatric milestone/referral map and short-answer reasoning.

units.title: Reproductive, sexual, and maternity care
objectives: Explain person-centered contraceptive counseling and the distinction between method eligibility and practice recommendations.
Identify the continuity and safety elements of prenatal, postpartum, and sexual-health care.
Recognize that procedures and obstetric deliveries require accredited supervision and cannot be learned from this course.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional counseling scenario to identify patient priorities and the authoritative resources to consult; no procedure teaching or individual medical advice.
units.assessment: Source-located counseling plan with uncertainty and referral/supervision triggers.

units.title: Common outpatient infection, stewardship, and outbreak recognition
objectives: Separate individual diagnostic reasoning from public-health notification and infection-control responsibilities.
Apply the stewardship framework of leadership, accountability, expertise, action, tracking, reporting, and education at a systems level.
Recognize archival outbreak recordings and return to current agency guidance for action.
units.casePractice: For a fictional urgent-care respiratory presentation, write questions that establish syndrome, severity, testing needs, and safety-net triggers before any antimicrobial choice.
units.assessment: Antibiotic-stewardship audit-and-feedback simulation and outbreak triage concept map.

units.title: Older-adult, home, and transitional care
objectives: Use the Screen–Assess–Intervene structure for fall-risk work at a conceptual level.
Integrate function, caregiver context, medication risk, and care transitions in a fictional geriatric case.
Distinguish clinical experience in home/long-term-care settings from lecture time.
units.casePractice: Complete a fictional fall-risk workflow using Screen–Assess–Intervene labels; list data that must be obtained by a qualified clinician.
units.assessment: Geriatric safety checklist and short reflective case analysis.

units.title: Musculoskeletal, skin, and office-procedure boundaries
objectives: Organize a safe musculoskeletal differential and identify red flags requiring escalation.
Describe why image review and procedures require supervision, competency assessment, and local governance.
Use authentic image resources only by their rights terms; never create diagnostic “patient scans.”
units.casePractice: Use the licensed, de-identified Open-i CXR collection only to practice observation and report comparison; do not upload, redistribute, or diagnose an individual image.
units.assessment: Image-rights checklist and fictional red-flag/referral reasoning exercise.

units.title: Urgent and emergent presentations and safety nets
objectives: Recognize that “urgent” is a time-to-action and safety-netting problem, not a list of diagnoses.
State escalation, handoff, and follow-up concepts for potentially unstable presentations.
Differentiate emergency department/ICU rotation exposure from self-study videos.
units.casePractice: Classify fictional vignettes by urgency and identify missing vital/sign/symptom information; no real-time triage or treatment instructions are provided.
units.assessment: Timed escalation-priority exercise with rationale.

units.title: Health equity, community partnership, telehealth, and advocacy
objectives: Identify structural and practical barriers that affect access, adherence, follow-up, and outcomes.
Design a small, non-patient-specific quality improvement measure that avoids blaming patients.
State privacy, access, and workflow questions raised by telehealth.
units.casePractice: Map a fictional missed-visit problem to transport, language, digital-access, and clinic-workflow contributors; propose a measurable system change.
units.assessment: Equity/QI storyboard and data-ethics reflection.

units.title: Practice transformation, informatics, and transition to supervised practice
objectives: Describe team roles, panel management, measurement, and evidence-to-workflow translation.
Critique an AI-enabled primary-care workflow for bias, validation, privacy, and human oversight.
State what this course cannot confer: credentials, clinical competence sign-off, board eligibility, or licensure.
units.casePractice: Write an implementation brief for a fictional reminder workflow, including a fairness/validation question and a clinician-oversight safeguard.
units.assessment: Capstone portfolio with evidence log, QI measure, and limits statement.

assignment.title: Fictional continuity-panel evidence portfolio
assignment.description: Complete three original, wholly fictional longitudinal vignettes: a preventive visit, a multimorbidity follow-up, and an urgent symptom contact. For each, state the decision question, identify current primary sources, quote no protected content, log source dates/caveats, identify missing information and escalation/supervision needs, and write a patient-centered follow-up concept. Add one non-patient-specific equity/QI storyboard. Do not use real patient records, submit to an institution, perform procedures, or represent the work as clinical documentation.
deliverables: Source/date ledger
three fictional reasoning maps
one quality-improvement storyboard
one reflection on course/residency/board-eligibility boundaries

assessment.summative: Portfolio reviewed only for educational completion by the learner; no clinical competency, certification, credits, CME, residency milestone, or board-passing prediction is awarded.
assessment.boardAlignment: The unit mapping follows ABFM’s published five domains. It is a curricular alignment aid only; no proprietary items, score prediction, or official ABFM endorsement is claimed.

studyHours.type: Transparent independent-study plan, not a residency-equivalent time claim
studyHours.note: Only observed accessible recording durations count toward video hours. Reading, cases, assessments, and planned clips do not count as verified video hours. No clinical rotation is counted as a lecture.

mapping.name: Tufts University Family Medicine Residency at CHA
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA’s official pages publish a three-year curriculum: outpatient team-based primary care, population health, complex care management, behavioral health/addictions, inpatient/community and tertiary experiences, leadership/improvement, and concentrations. The overview lists PGY rotation weeks and longitudinal experiences; descriptions include Family Medicine Center, evidence-based medicine, geriatrics, reproductive health, ICU, nursery, obstetrics, orthopaedics/sports medicine, pediatrics, and emergency medicine. CHA publishes a conference schedule but says it is subject to change; no proprietary lectures, recordings, case volumes, or unsourced didactic-hour total is claimed here.

medical.boardStatus: ABFM is the relevant ABMS member board for Family Medicine. Its certification process and its exam blueprint are separate from ACGME programme accreditation and from this self-study course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no ABFM eligibility, certification, board-eligible designation, ACGME credit, residency credit, degree, licensure, or clinical privileges. ABFM states that initial-certification training requires the stated MD/DO pathway and completion of 36 calendar months (12 months in each year) in an ACGME-accredited family medicine residency; the final two years must be in the same accredited programme for continuity. All training is subject to ABFM review before exam approval. The board-eligible period is a separate policy: seven years after successful completion of an ACGME-accredited family medicine residency, with continuing policy compliance. Verify individual status directly with ABFM.

officialProgrammes.name: Tufts University Family Medicine Residency at CHA
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA’s official pages publish a three-year curriculum: outpatient team-based primary care, population health, complex care management, behavioral health/addictions, inpatient/community and tertiary experiences, leadership/improvement, and concentrations. The overview lists PGY rotation weeks and longitudinal experiences; descriptions include Family Medicine Center, evidence-based medicine, geriatrics, reproductive health, ICU, nursery, obstetrics, orthopaedics/sports medicine, pediatrics, and emergency medicine. CHA publishes a conference schedule but says it is subject to change; no proprietary lectures, recordings, case volumes, or unsourced didactic-hour total is claimed here.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is an actual separate specialty programme, not a generic directory category: CHA labels it “Tufts University Family Medicine Residency at CHA.” The official site also calls CHA a teaching hospital of Harvard Medical School and Tufts School of Medicine. Source identity is preserved: this is not represented as a Harvard Medical School residency, a Johns Hopkins programme, or an official CHA recording collection. The supplied packet includes this one official institutional variant; no other institution is silently deduplicated into it.
sourceCaveats: CHA pages are a public programme description, not an assurance of current openings, accreditation status, individual rotation availability, conference topics, case volumes, or applicant eligibility. Check the programme directly.
ACGME requirements regulate accredited programmes. They do not validate this course or establish the status of any individual programme/learner.
ABFM eligibility/certification is separate from this learning plan; applicants/physicians must verify their own individual status with ABFM.

Public video availability and duration can change. Durations were observed as public metadata on the date checked, but no access is guaranteed, and no playback, CME, transcript, or content completeness assertion is made.

A duration is evidence that a recording is publicly listed, not proof that it is current, clinically appropriate for every learner, or sufficient to teach a topic. Current primary sources override archival/video content.
Open-i and PHIL rights vary by item. The course links to resources rather than rehosting images and forbids use of real patient records or fabricated synthetic diagnostic scans.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABFM blueprint domain has the largest targeted percentage of questions?

options.text: Preventive Care
Chronic Care Management
Acute Care and Diagnosis
Foundations of Care

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABFM lists Acute Care and Diagnosis at 35%, larger than Chronic Care Management (25%), Emergent and Urgent Care (20%), Preventive Care (15%), and Foundations of Care (5%). This is an original orientation question, not ABFM exam content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an archived immunization lecture that conflicts with a current schedule. What is the best study action?

options.text: Use the older lecture because it is longer.
Use the current CDC schedule page and verify the relevant notes; keep the lecture only for context.
Average the two recommendations.
Avoid documenting the discrepancy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Schedules change. The CDC schedule index is the current source and links to age- and condition-based schedules. An archived video can support concepts but cannot override current guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional well-child workflow, a caregiver’s milestone checklist raises concern. Which statement best reflects CDC guidance?

options.text: A checklist alone establishes a diagnosis.
Developmental monitoring replaces validated screening.
Developmental monitoring complements surveillance and does not replace standardized screening.
No follow-up is needed unless the family asks twice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC distinguishes monitoring, surveillance, and screening. Monitoring helps engage families but does not replace validated developmental screening or referral/follow-up when indicated.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional clinic wants to reduce outpatient antibiotic overuse. Which grouping is consistent with CDC’s 2026 outpatient stewardship framework?

options.text: Leadership commitment, accountability, expertise, action, tracking, reporting, and education
Only a one-time poster and patient handout
Automatic prescribing with no measurement
Replacing all clinical judgment with a chatbot

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes these structural and procedural elements. A stewardship programme uses measurement and feedback; it is not a single educational poster or an automated substitute for clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional older adult reports a recent fall. Which sequence names the CDC STEADI core elements?

options.text: Screen, Assess, Intervene
Diagnose, discharge, forget
Image, operate, rehabilitate
Prescribe, escalate, litigate

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC’s STEADI initiative is organized around Screen, Assess, and Intervene. The question tests framework recall, not a patient-specific risk determination.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the CDC 2022 opioid guideline’s stated limits?

options.text: It is an inflexible rule requiring rapid opioid tapering.
It replaces individualized clinical judgment.
It is intended for all pain, including cancer and end-of-life care.
It is a flexible outpatient adult pain-care guide and is not a substitute for individualized judgment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC explicitly says the guideline is flexible and should not be applied as inflexible standards or lead to rapid tapering/abrupt discontinuation. It excludes several pain contexts from its intended scope.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional prevention visit, which source is designed to list current USPSTF services receiving an A or B grade and their release dates?

options.text: The USPSTF A and B Recommendations index
A random social-media post
An undated conference slide
A specialty board examination recall

practiceQuestions.rationale: The live USPSTF A and B index states the topic, target population, grade, and release date. Current recommendations should be checked rather than inferred from an older summary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately separates this course from ABFM initial-certification eligibility?

options.text: Watching 36 hours of video substitutes for residency.
A self-study portfolio can grant board eligibility.
ABFM requires 36 calendar months in an ACGME-accredited family medicine residency, with 12 months in each training year.
Any clinical-related internet course grants licensure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABFM’s training page states the 36-calendar-month ACGME-accredited residency requirement, with 12 months in each training year. This independent course confers no training credit, eligibility, licensure, or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional applicant completed a qualifying accredited family medicine residency and asks how long the ABFM board-eligible period runs before additional requirements apply. What is the published period?

options.text: One year
Three years
Seven years
Unlimited

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABFM defines a seven-year period beginning after successful completion of an ACGME-accredited family medicine residency, subject to continuous policy compliance. This does not mean this course makes anyone eligible.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional trainee uses a public de-identified chest radiograph collection for image-literacy practice. What is the appropriate rights safeguard?

options.text: Rehost all images with no attribution because they are online.
Check the collection’s stated license and terms, attribute as required, and do not redistribute restricted material.
Create a synthetic scan and label it authentic.
Assume every image found through a search engine is public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NLM states that reuse depends on the individual source/license. Its Indiana University chest-x-ray collection is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and Open-i asks users to follow the applicable terms.

title: General Medicine Fellowship
level: Academic primary-care/general medicine research fellowship (directory-labelled; not a separate ABMS specialty)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Medical-school-level foundations in adult medicine, physiology, pharmacology, statistics and evidence appraisal are recommended.

For the actual fellowship, applicants are physicians screened on career goals and recommendations and one letter is from the current/most recent clinical training director; accepted fellows also apply separately to Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. This course does not administer or satisfy those requirements.
Ability to read current guidance critically and to use a supervisor/institutional process for any clinical, research, ethics, data-access or licensing question.
No patient contact, clinical procedure, prescription, use of protected health information, research enrolment, or dataset download is permitted or required by this independent study.
objectives: Accurately describe the actual BIDMC-linked programme as a two-year academic primary-care/general medicine research fellowship and state its credentialing boundaries.
Map broad adult general medicine study to the published ABIM Internal Medicine blueprint without claiming that it is an official course or exam predictor.
Formulate answerable clinical research questions and critique design, bias, uncertainty, reporting and applicability.
Use current primary prevention and chronic-disease sources with version/date checks rather than treating recordings as current guidance.
Explain consent, registry reporting, transparency, privacy/de-identification and image/case licensing boundaries.
Communicate a patient-centred problem representation, uncertainty and escalation needs using fictional cases only.
Prepare a transparent, fictional protocol/abstract/presentation that distinguishes evidence, inference, limitation and next step.

units.title: Programme identity, scope and research question
objectives: Distinguish the BIDMC directory label from the actual two-year Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research.
Frame a feasible general medicine/primary-care research question using population, exposure/intervention, comparator, outcome, setting and equity considerations.
boardDomains: Not a distinct General Medicine board; orientation to ABIM Internal Medicine broad-domain assessment and clinical epidemiology cross-cutting content
units.casePractice: Use a fictional clinic question about delayed follow-up after abnormal screening; write a one-sentence PECO and list two possible patient-important outcomes. No patient data are used.
units.assessment: Submit a 250-word question/rationale and a one-page scope statement that names what the fellowship is and is not.

units.title: Clinical epidemiology, bias and causal inference
objectives: Select a study design that matches an etiologic, prognostic, diagnostic or intervention question.
Identify confounding, selection bias, information bias, missingness and lack of transportability before interpreting an association.
boardDomains: Clinical Epidemiology (cross-cutting); ABIM tasks: assess risk/apply epidemiologic principles
units.casePractice: For a fictional EHR study of a new antihypertensive and falls, draw a causal diagram and specify one plausible confounder, one source of selection bias and one sensitivity analysis.
units.assessment: Methods worksheet scored for question-design alignment, bias identification and appropriate qualification of causal claims.

units.title: Biostatistics, evidence synthesis and transparent reporting
objectives: Interpret absolute risk, relative measures, confidence intervals and the distinction between precision and clinical importance.
Use CONSORT and a systematic-review methods guide to audit a fictional abstract without copying trial materials.
boardDomains: Clinical Epidemiology; Practice-Based Learning and Improvement
units.casePractice: Audit a fictional two-arm trial abstract for randomisation description, participant flow, outcome definition and harms reporting; do not infer unreported results.
units.assessment: Ten-item calculation/interpretation quiz plus a CONSORT-based structured critique.

units.title: Ethics, consent, data stewardship and dissemination
objectives: Explain why human-subjects protections and legally effective consent are processes rather than forms.
Separate IRB/ethics obligations, trial registration/results reporting and publication reporting standards.
units.casePractice: Review a fictional patient-information sheet for missing plain-language explanation of purpose, risks, voluntariness and contacts. This is not an IRB submission.
units.assessment: Ethics memo: identify three issues and name the institutional/IRB question that requires supervised review.

units.title: Prevention, screening, vaccination and equitable primary care
objectives: Use a structured age/condition/notes/contraindication workflow rather than memorising a partial vaccine table.
Explain that preventive recommendations depend on population, benefit-harm balance and availability of follow-up.
boardDomains: Prevention; Cardiovascular Disease; Medical Oncology; Geriatric Syndromes; Obstetrics and Gynecology
units.casePractice: For a fictional 66-year-old with incomplete records, write the information that must be checked before applying the CDC schedule; do not prescribe or administer anything.
units.assessment: Preventive-care evidence table with source/version/date and explicit limits.

units.title: Cardiometabolic disease and risk communication
objectives: Prioritise risk, symptoms, medication context and patient goals when interpreting common cardiometabolic presentations.
Identify how diabetes, kidney disease, obesity and cardiovascular risk interact without substituting a recording for current guidance.
units.casePractice: Interpret a fictional longitudinal record showing a new elevated A1C and competing cardiovascular risk factors; state what requires confirmation and what patient-centred questions belong in an assessment.
units.assessment: Single-best-answer formative questions plus a short evidence-update note that cites the 2026 ADA Standards, not a lecture date.

units.title: Pulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal and infectious presentations
objectives: Organise undifferentiated dyspnea, kidney dysfunction, gastrointestinal symptoms and infection risk by acuity and diagnostic uncertainty.
Recognise that infection-prevention and antimicrobial decisions require current local and national guidance.
units.casePractice: Create a problem representation for a fictional immunocompromised adult with dyspnea and abnormal kidney tests, explicitly separating urgent possibilities from testable hypotheses. No treatment plan is requested.
units.assessment: Problem-representation rubric and evidence-source log.

units.title: Hematology, oncology, allergy and rheumatology
objectives: Differentiate a symptom-based problem representation from a definitive diagnosis in complex inflammatory or malignant presentations.
Appraise how age, comorbidity and medication burden affect general-medicine coordination.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional older adult with fatigue, adenopathy and multiple medicines to list a differential category, safety flags and questions for specialist co-management; do not select chemotherapy or dosage.
units.assessment: Structured differential and evidence-hierarchy worksheet.

units.title: Neurology, dermatology, psychiatry, substance use and aging
objectives: Recognise high-stakes neurologic and dermatologic presentations that merit timely supervised evaluation.
Incorporate cognition, polypharmacy, palliative needs and substance-use stigma into a patient-centred problem list.
boardDomains: Palliative and End-of-Life Care; Substance Abuse (cross-cutting)
units.casePractice: Create a de-identified, fictional safety-oriented handoff for an older adult with new confusion and a medication change; identify what must be escalated to a supervising clinician.
units.assessment: Handoff checklist and reflective note on uncertainty, bias and communication.

units.title: Medication safety, pharmacoepidemiology and comparative effectiveness
objectives: Explain why exposure definition, new-user/active-comparator choices and time zero matter in drug-outcomes research.
Distinguish efficacy, effectiveness, comparative safety, access and cost questions.
boardDomains: Clinical Epidemiology; Patient Safety; Systems-Based Practice
units.casePractice: Specify a fictional active-comparator, new-user cohort question about a commonly used medication class. State why a prevalent-user design could mislead.
units.assessment: One-page protocol skeleton; it is not an approval to access EHR, claims, or patient data.

units.title: Health systems, quality improvement, health equity and implementation
objectives: Distinguish research, quality improvement and clinical operations before choosing oversight and dissemination paths.
Use a process map to identify a measurable care-delivery inequity without attributing outcomes to a group identity.
boardDomains: Health Equity; Systems-Based Practice; Practice-Based Learning and Improvement
units.casePractice: Build a fictional clinic workflow map for missed blood-pressure follow-up. Identify one process measure, one outcome measure, and one unintended consequence.
units.assessment: QI/research boundary memo and equity-impact reflection.

units.title: Scholarship synthesis, presentation and career boundaries
objectives: Prepare a transparent research abstract and oral update that separates findings, limitations and next steps.
State accurately why this study course and the actual fellowship do not confer residency credit, board eligibility, licensure or an MD/DO degree.
boardDomains: Practice-Based Learning and Improvement; Professionalism; no separate General Medicine board
units.casePractice: Deliver a five-minute mock conference presentation of a fictional study and a two-minute limitations statement. No real patient data or invented results.
units.assessment: Capstone protocol/analysis plan, lay summary, and oral presentation scored with a transparency-and-limits rubric.

assignment.title: Fictional general-medicine research protocol and evidence brief
deliverables: One-page PECO/PICO question and causal/bias map.
2–3-page protocol skeleton: population, data boundary, exposure/comparator, outcomes, confounding plan, missing-data plan, equity considerations and limitations.
CONSORT- or AHRQ-informed critique of a fictional abstract; no proprietary questions or copied article text.
One-page prevention/clinical-source update log that records source version/date and states what needs supervised confirmation.
Five-minute presentation plus a 250-word plain-language summary.
assignment.safeguards: Use entirely fictional/de-identified scenarios. Do not collect, upload or analyse real patient data; do not submit to an IRB or registry through this course; do not claim that the work has ethical approval or clinical validity.

summative.passingStatement: No score is a board-passing prediction or certification. Assessment is self-study feedback; a clinician/educator should review any real clinical or research work.

studyHours.statement: This is a transparent independent-study plan, not an estimate of the fellowship’s clinical training time. The 36-hour video floor is met only by the deduplicated ready-recording ledger.

mapping.name: Harvard Medical School Fellowship in General Medicine and Primary Care / Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: BIDMC presents the two-year academic fellowship as research training in general medicine: clinical research methods, statistical analysis, research collaboration, teaching/public speaking and clinician-investigator preparation. Its Division page separately lists it among research fellowships.

mapping.institution: Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research (multi-site programme)
mapping.name: Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The programme calls itself a two-year programme for physicians pursuing academic medicine and research. Its public home page lists BIDMC, BWH Pharmacoepidemiology/Pharmacoeconomics, The Cambridge Hospital, Department of Population Medicine (HMS/Harvard Pilgrim), and Massachusetts General Brigham as participating sites. These are sites/variants within the one fellowship, not separately verified board specialties.

mapping.name: Participating Harvard Fellowship site
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Public site description: dedicated faculty mentor, weekly site-director meetings, and research in primary care/inpatient general medicine, including population health, equity, quality improvement and data-based research.

mapping.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Division of Pharmacoepidemiology and Pharmacoeconomics
mapping.name: Participating Harvard Fellowship site
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Public site description: prescription drug use/policy, evidence-based medication use, comparative safety/effectiveness, pharmacoepidemiology, health services research and medication outcomes.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent study and the two-year research fellowship do not themselves make a learner eligible for ABIM certification. Rules can change and ABIM decides eligibility at application. medical.programmeSourceScope: Transparent scope finding: the declared BIDMC “General Medicine Fellowship” page is a directory-level label that links to an actual two-year, research-focused Harvard Fellowship in General Medicine and Primary Care / Primary Care Research. It is not a generic board specialty, not a separate ACGME clinical subspecialty established by this page, and not a nuclear medicine/radiology programme. The public programme publishes research training, a summer academic core and limited continuity clinical work; it does not publish a complete lecture catalogue, case volumes, procedure requirements, an ACGME accreditation claim, or a separate board exam.
sourceCaveats: Source identities are kept separate: BIDMC/HMS pages describe the fellowship; ABIM/ABMS sources describe certification/blueprints; ACGME describes accredited-training standards; CDC/USPSTF/ADA describe current clinical guidance; YouTube listings describe external recordings. None authenticates the others.

The supplied outline concerns nuclear medicine/radiology, therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, imaging AI and unsupported volume/dual-board assertions. It is out of scope for MED-045 and was not imported as curriculum, programme fact, certification, clinical rotation, or indication.

Video durations were observed in public YouTube search metadata on 2026-10-07. Direct metadata probes later encountered YouTube bot/rate blocks. Links, titles, free status and durations should be rechecked before use; a recording is not a current clinical authority.

Public fellowship pages do not publish a full lecture inventory, clinical case volume, procedures, ACGME status for this exact research fellowship, or a separate board examination. Those facts are intentionally not inferred.

MedPix’s landing page carried a government funding/status warning during review. Its reuse terms were not exposed in the public extraction, so it is link-only pending case-specific rights verification.
This course contains no real patient records, diagnostic scans, fabricated patient images, proprietary questions, protected downloads, subscriptions, payments or exam content.

Draw exposure, confounder, outcome and censoring paths.
Explain why a statistical model cannot repair an ill-defined question.
State that no dataset access is authorised.
originalClipPlan.gapRationale: Ready recordings include biostatistics but do not provide a concise, current programme-site-specific pharmacoepidemiology bias walkthrough.

originalClipPlan.title: How to use a prevention source without turning a table into a prescription
objectives: Apply the CDC schedule workflow conceptually.
State why condition, contraindication, local context and shared decision-making must be checked.
scriptOutline: Show a conceptual workflow, not vaccine doses or individual advice.
Use a fictional incomplete record.
Identify source date/version and refer learners to current notes/addendum.
Close with limits and supervision statement.
originalClipPlan.gapRationale: The ready lectures are dated or broad; none substitutes for a short source-versioned navigation lesson for the current CDC/USPSTF workflow.

originalClipPlan.title: Consent, reporting and dissemination: three separate obligations
objectives: Differentiate consent, registration/results reporting and trial-reporting guidance.
Recognise when an IRB/institutional review is needed.

Compare three obligations in a non-legal educational diagram.
Do not promise legal compliance.
Close with actual-study escalation paths.

originalClipPlan.title: Transparent clinical reasoning under uncertainty: problem representation and safety-netting
objectives: Create a problem representation rather than prematurely label a diagnosis.
State escalation and safety-netting limits in a fictional vignette.

Avoid a treatment order, dosing or real-patient advice.
Close with supervision/emergency-care reminder.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 66-year-old with incomplete immunization records is discussed in a classroom vignette. Before applying an adult vaccine recommendation, which sequence best reflects the CDC schedule workflow?

options.text: Choose a vaccine by age alone, then add doses if records are missing.
Determine age-based recommendations, assess medical-condition/other indications, review notes, then review contraindications/precautions.
Use a historical schedule because it is simpler to memorise.
Defer all preventive decisions until a specialty consultation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CDC page explicitly directs clinicians to determine by age, assess conditions/other indications, review notes, and review contraindications/precautions. This question tests workflow only; it does not direct patient care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional asymptomatic adult has a single laboratory A1C result in the diabetes range. Which next interpretation is most defensible for study purposes?

options.text: A single abnormal result always confirms a diagnosis without any context.
Diagnostic interpretation should follow the current ADA diagnosis/classification standards, including confirmation requirements when appropriate.
The result can be ignored because only symptoms matter.
A dated board-review video is more authoritative than a current guideline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ADA Standards of Care provides current diagnostic/classification guidance and is updated regularly. The course avoids converting one fictional value into an individual diagnosis or treatment order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A research team compares an antihypertensive started this month with a medication started years earlier, then observes falls. Which design concern is most important to raise before accepting a causal conclusion?

options.text: Whether exposure groups have different baseline risk and time-zero definitions, creating confounding and time-related bias.
Whether the abstract has a colourful figure.
Whether every person has the same outcome.
Whether no study question was written.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AHRQ’s methods guidance supports explicit question/design/bias appraisal. Baseline prognosis, exposure definition and follow-up time can materially distort observational associations.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional randomised trial manuscript, which missing element most directly limits a reader’s ability to follow participants through the study?

options.text: A participant-flow description.
The authors’ preferred font.
A hospital logo.
A claim that randomisation eliminates all uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CONSORT 2025 is a reporting guideline for randomised trials; participant flow is central to transparent reporting. A report can still have limitations even when randomisation is used.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner says, “We collected signatures, so the human-subjects consent process is complete.” Which response is best?

options.text: Correct; a signature alone replaces all other protections.
Consent and human-subject protections require attention to the applicable regulations, information, voluntariness and institutional/IRB oversight; a course cannot make that determination.
Consent is unnecessary for all minimal-risk research.
ClinicalTrials.gov registration automatically substitutes for consent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: OHRP supplies consent guidance within a wider human-subject-protection framework. Real protocol decisions require the responsible institution/IRB and current applicable requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sponsor asks whether a proposed FDA-regulated trial must be registered and submit results. What is the best first action?

options.text: Assume every study has identical requirements.
Check the study’s applicability, responsible party and current legal/policy requirements using ClinicalTrials.gov guidance and institutional support.
Wait until publication is accepted.
Use a course completion certificate as authorisation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ClinicalTrials.gov describes several legal and policy pathways and the Final Rule scope. Applicability is study-specific; this course does not make a legal determination.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABIM Internal Medicine blueprint category carries the largest approximate percentage of a typical certification examination?

options.text: Cardiovascular Disease (14%).
Ophthalmology (1%).
Allergy and Immunology (2%).
Geriatric Syndromes (3%).

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published ABIM blueprint assigns approximately 14% to Cardiovascular Disease. Percentages are approximate for a typical examination and may vary; this is not an ABIM question.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner asks whether completing the two-year Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research alone makes them eligible for the ABIM Internal Medicine Certification Examination. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Yes; any two-year general medicine fellowship replaces residency.
No. ABIM requires the applicable predoctoral, licensing and accredited internal medicine residency requirements; subspecialty fellowship training does not credit the residency requirement.
Yes, if the learner watches 36 hours of video.
Yes, if a research mentor signs an abstract.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM’s policy states that 36 months of accredited internal medicine residency are required and that subspecialty fellow training cannot credit that internal medicine training requirement. The BIDMC-linked programme is research-focused and two years.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description best characterises the clinical component published for the Harvard Fellowship in Primary Care Research?

options.text: A full-time clinical rotation schedule that supplies lecture hours.
A primarily research-focused programme in which each fellow typically provides general internal medicine care for one half-day per week at an affiliated practice.
An unsupervised substitute for residency.
A separate ABMS specialty certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official clinical-experience page says the programme is primarily research-focused and fellows typically have a half-day per week of general internal medicine care. Clinical practice is not counted in this course’s video total.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching team plans to copy a Radiopaedia case into a paywalled course without attribution. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Proceed because all free-to-view clinical images are public domain.
Do not proceed without appropriate permission; Radiopaedia states CC BY-NC-SA terms, attribution requirements and restrictions on paid/paywalled use.
Remove the patient age and publish it without source attribution.
Replace it with an AI-generated image and call it a diagnostic case.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia’s licence requires attribution and noncommercial/share-alike conditions and specifically warns that paid/paywalled course use is not automatically permitted. This course links only and does not create diagnostic ground truth from generated images.

title: Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship — actual named ACGME-accredited Johns Hopkins programme; this entry is an independent self-study adaptation.-aligned independent study
prerequisites: For actual Hopkins fellowship: completion of an ACGME-accredited internal medicine or family practice residency is the published application threshold; current board eligibility is separately governed by ABIM/ABFM.
For advanced independent study: adult-medicine, pharmacology, physical examination, evidence-interpretation and safe-escalation foundations.
No learner should use this course to diagnose, prescribe, undertake procedures, handle real patient records or represent themselves as a fellow/geriatrician.
objectives: Synthesize a person-centered comprehensive geriatric assessment using function, cognition, mobility, medication and life goals.
Reason through common disease and multifactorial geriatric syndromes while stating uncertainty and escalation needs.
Apply published delirium, fall-risk and medication-review frameworks without treating them as automatic orders.
Compare care settings and explain why continuity, interprofessional teams and supervision matter.
Discuss capacity, surrogate decision-making, caregiver concerns, prevention, palliative care, equity and quality improvement with appropriate boundaries.

units.title: Gerontology, comprehensive assessment and What Matters

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Geriatric Medicine Certification
American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) — Certificate of Added Qualification (CAQ) in Geriatric Medicine
medical.boardStatus: ABIM describes a jointly developed ABIM/ABFM Geriatric Medicine Certification Examination, administered by ABIM. For internists it is ABIM subspecialty certification; for family physicians ABFM calls its credential a CAQ. Neither is a separate Gerontology board certificate. The August 2026 ABIM blueprint is used only for transparent curriculum mapping.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no credential, affiliation, ACGME credit, board eligibility, licensure, procedure authorization or certification. Current ABIM policy requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification at application, requisite accredited fellowship, documented competence/ethical behavior, a valid unrestricted/un­challenged medical license, and a passing examination; ABIM lists 12 training months, all clinical. Current ABFM CAQ requirements state continuous family medicine certification, ≥12 months full-time in an ACGME-accredited fellowship, application/fees and a passing one-day exam. Follow live ABIM/ABFM policies. Johns Hopkins uses legacy “ABFP” wording; the current board is ABFM.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 82-year-old has sudden fluctuation in attention and awareness one day after admission; family says cognition was normal last week. Best first framing?

options.text: Assume chronic dementia and defer assessment.
Treat as possible delirium and arrange prompt assessment for contributors and safety.
Conclude depression because of age.
Start a long-term cognitive medicine without evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute fluctuating attention is a delirium pattern and needs prompt clinical evaluation; this course authorizes no orders.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 76-year-old takes a drug class listed in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. Best next learning action?

options.text: Tell the person to stop immediately.
Use it to review indication, alternatives, risks, goals, kidney function and monitoring with the prescribing team.
Ignore it because all older adults tolerate drugs alike.
Assume every listed drug is forbidden in hospice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Criteria flag potentially inappropriate medicines and support—not replace—shared decision-making; they are not automatic stop orders and have stated scope limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional community-dwelling 79-year-old reports a fall and fear of falling. Which modifiable domains fit CDC STEADI?

options.text: Gait/balance, medicines, orthostasis, vision, feet/footwear and home hazards.
Only head CT and an age cut-off.
Only bone density testing.
Only a promise not to fall.

practiceQuestions.rationale: STEADI uses Screen–Assess–Intervene and names these domains for individualized assessment/intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional inpatient repeats a proposed procedure but cannot consistently explain how risks/benefits apply to their own goals. What needs focused clinical assessment?

options.text: Decision-specific capacity.
Global incapacity due to age.
Automatic transfer of all decisions to family.
A board-exam score.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific; age alone does not determine it. Follow local law and supervising clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 84-year-old says walking to the garden with a spouse matters most. Best 4Ms response?

options.text: Document goal and examine medication, mentation and mobility barriers in relation to it.
Avoid goals because diseases are objective.
Focus only on one laboratory value.
Promise every intervention restores prior function.

practiceQuestions.rationale: 4Ms integrates What Matters with Medication, Mentation and Mobility; it does not guarantee outcomes.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which experience is explicitly required in current ACGME Geriatric Medicine requirements?

options.text: 12 months longitudinal LTC clinical experience managing assigned panel as primary practitioner.
A fixed number of video lectures instead of clinical care.
A required procedure-case minimum.
Only one short facility visit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires 12 months longitudinal LTC with assigned panel. This independent course cannot provide it.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 73-year-old has unintentional weight loss, a new fall and urgency. Best initial reasoning stance?

options.text: Treat each as unrelated until one diagnosis is proven.
Use multifactorial geriatric-syndrome assessment while evaluating red flags and contributors.
Assume normal aging; no evaluation.
Select a medication before history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Geriatric syndromes often have multiple causes and systems; red flags still need clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 86-year-old has chronic memory impairment and abrupt inattention after a medicine change. Best statement?

options.text: Dementia makes delirium impossible.
Consider superimposed delirium and escalate for assessment.
Memory impairment proves cause.
Collateral history is useless.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Delirium can occur with baseline cognitive impairment; acute change/attention require evaluation and collateral history.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects ABIM pathway for an internist?

options.text: Watching this course creates eligibility.
Prior ABIM IM certification, accredited fellowship, unrestricted license, documented competence and passing exam are required.
A gerontology lecture series substitutes for fellowship.
No clinical fellowship months required.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are ABIM requirements, with 12 listed training/clinical months. Self-study is not an eligibility route.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional discharge plan has diagnoses/medicine names but omits baseline function, caregiver capacity and follow-up owner. Best improvement?

options.text: Add function, What Matters, medication questions, caregiver/support needs, team roles and named follow-up.
Delete social/functional information.
Assume next setting reconstructs it.
Replace team communication with video link.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires care across settings and 4Ms emphasizes goal-focused integration across transitions.

title: Gerontology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship directory wrapper; transparent study scope: Geriatric Medicine-aligned independent study
prerequisites: For intended physician-fellow level: completion of a supervised Internal Medicine or Family Medicine residency is the BIDMC stated entry prerequisite; learners outside that pathway may study concepts but do not become fellowship/board eligible.
Working knowledge of adult history, physical examination, medication reconciliation, common internal/family medicine conditions, basic evidence appraisal, and patient-safety principles.
A supervised clinical environment is required for real patient assessment, prescribing, capacity evaluations, procedures, and care transitions.
objectives: Use comprehensive geriatric assessment to integrate disease, function, cognition, medications, social context, environment, and patient goals.
Reason through geriatric syndromes including falls, frailty, delirium, cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, incontinence, weight loss, pressure injury, and deconditioning.
Adapt disease management to multimorbidity, functional reserve, prognosis uncertainty, patient priorities, and care setting.
Plan safe, person-centred transitions across clinic, hospital, post-acute, long-term care, home, and hospice settings.
Apply ethical, communication, capacity, caregiver, and palliative-care principles in fictional educational cases.
Critically interpret aging research and develop a limited QI, policy, research, or clinician-educator proposal without real patient data.

units.title: Scope, normal aging, and comprehensive geriatric assessment
objectives: Distinguish normal age-related physiologic change from disease and functional decline.
Construct a problem list that incorporates medical, functional, cognitive, mood, medication, social, and goal domains.
topics: demography, living arrangement, disability and social context
units.casePractice: Create a CGA map for a fictional 82-year-old, identifying missing collateral history and reversible contributors.
units.assessment: Five-item short-answer CGA synthesis.

units.title: Prevention, health equity, and age-friendly person-centred care
objectives: Apply preventive, screening, and vaccination thinking while considering life expectancy, burden, goals, and access.
Elicit what matters to a person and identify inequities or practical barriers that change a care plan.
units.casePractice: Write a goal-concordant preventive-care discussion for a fictional older adult with multimorbidity; do not use age alone as a decision rule.
units.assessment: Brief reflective plan graded for patient goals, risks, and support needs.

units.title: Medication safety, pharmacology, and deprescribing
objectives: Explain age-related pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic vulnerability and identify high-risk medication patterns.
Perform a goal-aligned medication review that considers indication, benefit, harm, burden, renal function, and monitoring.
units.casePractice: For a fictional medication list, identify three questions to resolve before any change and draft shared-decision language.
units.assessment: Medication-review note with stated uncertainty and follow-up monitoring.

units.title: Frailty, falls, mobility, osteoporosis, and rehabilitation
objectives: Stratify falls risk and recognize when multifactorial assessment is indicated.
Integrate gait, strength, orthostasis, medication, sensory, environment, fear-of-falling, and fracture-risk considerations into a tailored plan.
units.casePractice: Use the CC BY 4.0 linked falls case only as a reading; create a new fictional risk map rather than copying patient data or images.
units.assessment: Structured falls plan; assess risk factors, evidence-supported referrals, and return precautions.

units.title: Acute illness, delirium, and perioperative/inpatient geriatrics
objectives: Differentiate acute, fluctuating delirium from chronic cognitive impairment and depression using history from an informant.
Prioritize evaluation of acute contributors and non-pharmacologic prevention/management while avoiding restraints as routine care.
boardDomains: Diseases in the Elderly—Infectious, Neurology, Cardiovascular
units.casePractice: Complete the open standardized-patient delirium exercise only as simulation; label it constructed, not a real patient case.
units.assessment: Single-best-answer questions plus an informant-history checklist.

units.title: Cognition, dementia, depression, behavior, and caregiver partnership
objectives: Select a brief cognitive tool appropriately and explain why a positive screen requires further evaluation rather than a diagnosis.
Formulate a dementia-care plan including function, safety, behavioral symptoms, caregiver capacity, and referral needs.
units.casePractice: Use the published dementia case by link only; identify which facts are context-specific and should not be generalized.
units.assessment: Cognitive-care-plan checklist and vignette questions.

units.title: Mood, pain, sleep, sensory loss, continence, nutrition, and common geriatric syndromes
objectives: Recognize syndromic presentations and co-occurrence rather than pursuing a single-cause explanation prematurely.
Propose function-preserving, interdisciplinary first steps for pain, mood, sleep, sensory, continence, and nutrition concerns.
boardDomains: Geriatric Syndromes—Incontinence, Pressure ulcers, Sleep, Undernutrition
units.casePractice: Build a fictional symptom-network diagram that includes medication, function, caregiver, and environment contributors.
units.assessment: Problem-representation exercise; faculty/rubric feedback recommended.

units.title: Common disease management and atypical presentation in older adults
objectives: Adapt diagnostic reasoning for multimorbidity, functional reserve, goals, and atypical presentations without using age as a shortcut.
Integrate cardiovascular, endocrine, infectious, renal, neurologic, pulmonary, and musculoskeletal risks into a prioritized plan.
boardDomains: Diseases in the Elderly (45%)—all organ-system subsections
units.casePractice: Prioritize a fictional older patient’s competing problems using time sensitivity, burden, function, and stated preferences.
units.assessment: Clinical-reasoning grid with rationale and safety-net.

units.title: Care settings, long-term care, home care, PACE, and transitions
objectives: Compare the needs and risks of ambulatory, acute, rehabilitation, long-term-care, home, hospice, and community settings.
Design a transition plan that assigns medication reconciliation, functional supports, follow-up, and caregiver communication.
boardDomains: Caring for Elderly Patients—Health care delivery models (2%)
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional hospital-to-home transition plan with accountable roles; do not claim it substitutes for clinical supervision.
units.assessment: Transition-of-care note and team handoff rubric.

units.title: Capacity, ethics, serious-illness communication, and palliative care
objectives: Separate decision-making capacity from diagnosis, global competence, and family preference; describe task-specific assessment.
Conduct a goals-of-care conversation that incorporates prognosis uncertainty, surrogate role, symptom needs, and values.
boardDomains: Caring for Elderly Patients—Ethics, Decision making, Palliative care (5%)
units.casePractice: Use the linked, consented memory-clinic driving case as a discussion prompt; account for jurisdictional variation and do not give individual legal advice.
units.assessment: Observed structured discussion using a fictional scenario; self-assessment against communication checklist.

units.title: Scholarship, quality improvement, policy, and clinician-educator development
objectives: Critically appraise an aging-related intervention, identifying population, outcome, limitations, and implementation constraints.
Develop a small, ethical, non-patient-data quality-improvement or education proposal connected to an older-adult care gap.
boardDomains: Caring for Elderly Patients—Economic aspects/Delivery models
units.casePractice: Submit a two-page QI, policy, research, or educator-track proposal with a logic model and no real patient data.
units.assessment: Proposal scored with transparency, feasibility, ethics, and evidence-use rubric.

assignment.title: Goal-aligned comprehensive geriatric assessment and transition portfolio
deliverables: A fictional CGA and prioritised problem representation.
A medication-review reasoning table that identifies questions, benefits/harms, and monitoring—not medication orders.
A falls/delirium/cognition risk map with evidence links.
A fictional transition or long-term-care team handoff with caregiver and follow-up roles.
A two-page scholarly, policy, QI, or educator-track proposal.
assignment.sourceRules: Use only fictional cases created by the learner or the linked sources. Do not upload, include, or infer from real patient records, images, identifiers, or proprietary test items. Published cases are linked for discussion, not copied or treated as a patient chart.
assignment.grading: Rubric: evidence and uncertainty 30%, function/goals/caregiver integration 25%, safety and escalation boundaries 25%, communication and equity 10%, source and privacy discipline 10%.

formative: Unit quizzes: original single-best-answer questions and short reasoning prompts.
Faculty/peer-feedback-ready checklists for CGA, delirium assessment, medication review, capacity discussion, and transitions.
Self-audit against source boundaries and no-real-patient-data rule.
assessment.summative: Portfolio rubric plus 30 original questions. This is not an ABIM/ABFM examination, a validated predictor of passing, or an official programme assessment.
assessment.passingClaim: No score confers clinical competence, credit, certification, board eligibility, licensure, or guaranteed examination success.

studyHours.plan: A 68-hour independent-study plan: 39.8217 verified public video hours; 16 hours readings/case analysis; 8 hours assignment/portfolio; 4 hours original question review; 0.8 hour planned supplemental clips if they are later produced.
studyHours.importantBoundary: The 39.8217 hours is media runtime, not clinical training. Planned clips are excluded from verified hours. No rotation, patient-care, or case volume is counted as lecture time.

mapping.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School Multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship
mapping.name: Gerontology Fellowship (directory label); Harvard Medical School Multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship (actual clinical programme)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: BIDMC states that the Division of Gerontology sponsors the ACGME-accredited multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship. The public overview names BIDMC, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Element Care (PACE), Hebrew SeniorLife, Mount Auburn Hospital, and VA Boston Healthcare System; it describes exposure to primary care, house calls, institutional long-term care, skilled nursing, weekly half-day education, interdisciplinary teamwork, finance/policy, leadership, cultural care, and underserved outreach. It does not publish a complete lecture inventory or didactic-hour total.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship directory wrapper; transparent study scope: Geriatric Medicine
boardNames: ABFM Certificate of Added Qualification (CAQ) in Geriatric Medicine—jointly offered examination context, separate ABFM eligibility route
medical.boardStatus: BIDMC’s directory label “Gerontology Fellowship” links to the ACGME-accredited Harvard Medical School Multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship. “Gerontology” is not presented here as a separate ABMS board specialty or separate certification. ABIM and ABFM jointly develop the Geriatric Medicine examination; ABIM administers it to candidates from both boards. ABFM calls its credential a CAQ.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: For the ABIM route, current policy requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification at application, requisite accredited Geriatric Medicine fellowship training, clinical competence/ethical conduct, a valid unrestricted unchallenged license, and a passing examination. Training must be ACGME, RCPSC, or CMQ accredited; ABIM lists 12 total and 12 clinical months, with training complete by October 31 of the exam year. For ABFM initial CAQ, continuously maintained family medicine certification, at least 12 months full-time ACGME-accredited Geriatric Medicine fellowship with verification, application, and passing the one-day examination are required. This course supplies none of those requirements and neither determines nor confers eligibility.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: BIDMC states that the Division of Gerontology sponsors the ACGME-accredited multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship. The public overview names BIDMC, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Element Care (PACE), Hebrew SeniorLife, Mount Auburn Hospital, and VA Boston Healthcare System; it describes exposure to primary care, house calls, institutional long-term care, skilled nursing, weekly half-day education, interdisciplinary teamwork, finance/policy, leadership, cultural care, and underserved outreach. It does not publish a complete lecture inventory or didactic-hour total.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The declared page is a programme directory/wrapper titled “Gerontology Fellowship,” not evidence of a distinct “Gerontology” certification. Its detailed linked page identifies one actual ACGME clinical physician programme: the HMS Multicampus Geriatric Medicine Fellowship. This independent course covers the published Geriatric Medicine scope and preserves BIDMC’s research, clinician-educator, and health-care-policy advanced-track descriptions as variants, rather than inventing separate clinical subspecialties.
sourceCaveats: All official programme, board, ACGME, CMS, CDC, NICE, NIH, HRSA, VA, and case pages were read from their source URLs on 2026-10-07. Current policies and guidelines may change; use the source page at point of care or application.

originalClipPlan.title: Medication review without a “stop list”: indication, goals, and monitoring
objectives: Show a structured medication-review sequence.
